mutants.title: 48-Hour Verify List for Independent Floorplan Lenders
mutants.one_liner: A daily, capacity-capped list of the specific floored VINs an independent lender's auditor should physically verify in the next 48 hours, built from listing disappearance plus the lender's own payoff ledger, with a disposition classifier and per-dealer baselines that fix the noisy-signal problem.
mutants.customer: Head of collateral or audit (CRO as signer) at independent used-car floorplan lenders with roughly $30M to $500M outstanding across 100 to 1,500 independent and buy-here-pay-here dealers, plus credit unions and community banks with dealer floorplan lines. It deliberately excludes franchised new-car dealers, where captives already get retail delivery reports and can build this in-house. Secondary channel is regional floorplan audit firms that dispatch for-cause audits.
mutants.problem: An independent lender has a handful of auditors and hundreds of dealers, so the Monday question is not 'is there fraud' but 'which 12 VINs at which 4 dealers do I visit this week'. The judges' flaws map onto this. (1) A raw 'VIN left the website' flag is noisy, since the car may be wholesaled, transferred to a sister lot, in recon or never listed. (2) A fixed 7 to 10 day payoff window misfires on slow-funding but honest dealers. (3) A standalone radar dashboard is one more screen for a team with no data scientists. (4) The $15 to $30 per dealer price is unvalidated. (5) It misses double-flooring, which was most of Sky Auto Mall.
mutants.solution: Data need is one file: the lender's daily list of active floored VINs (VIN, dealer, floor date, advance), exported as a flat file from any core system. A VIN dropping off that file means it was paid, so no payoff-event integration is needed. Listing history comes from a licensed feed (a MarketCheck-type source scanning 100k+ dealer sites daily), plus a crawl of only the lender's own dealers' public sites, which the lender's dealer agreement can require them to permit. (a) A disposition classifier sorts every vanished floored VIN into transfer to a sister store, appears at auction or wholesale, relisted, or 'retail-sale signature' (gone, no reappearance, often after a pending or price-change state). Only the last type with an open balance enters the queue. (b) Each dealer gets its own baseline lag distribution of delist-to-payoff days learned over 90 days, and the flag fires on deviation from that dealer's own pattern, not a fixed window. (c) The output is capped to the lender's audit capacity, for example 'you have 3 auditor-days: here are the 12 VINs at 4 dealers with the highest expected loss', with a timestamped listing-history evidence pack and a one-click verify request that can go to the lender's own auditors or an audit vendor. (d) An optional second signal is title or lien-release data where lawfully obtainable, but v1 does not depend on it.
mutants.why_now: Tricolor and PrimaLend (Sept 2025) and the Sky Auto Mall litigation (Ford Credit and Stellantis, March 2026) made every lender's risk committee ask what they know between audits. Inventory sits near 88 days' supply with floorplan at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps, so dealers lean harder on lines. Licensed daily dealer-site listing history now exists off the shelf, and LLM extraction makes normalizing messy dealer pages cheap for a team of three. Vero's April 2026 content says bank dealer-services teams want to 'automate audit triage and SOT reporting', which confirms the buyer's framing.
mutants.revenue_model: Platform fee of about $1,500 to $3,000 per month per lender, sized to dealer count and booked against the audit budget, plus a catch fee of about $250 per VIN later confirmed unpaid-sold by the lender's own ledger and caught before its next scheduled audit. A backtest-based 'retro-scan' is priced at $5k and credited against year one. A lender with 300 dealers pays roughly $40k to $60k per year. A first-two-years target of 40 to 60 lenders and credit unions implies roughly $2M to $3.5M ARR. These are assumptions to validate, not findings.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The lender's payoff ledger is free data hiding in plain sight: a VIN leaving the daily floored-VIN file is the payoff event, so the product needs one CSV, not a core-system integration. The real product is dispatch, not detection. Auditors only pay for a signal that changes whom they visit this week, and the noise is tamed by comparing each dealer to its own delist-to-payoff habits rather than to a global threshold, and by refusing to alert unless the disposition looks like a retail sale.
mutants.first_30_days: Weeks 1 to 2, backtest on public cases (Sky Auto Mall filings and a few others) using historical listing data to show fire dates versus discovery dates. In parallel, interview five lender audit or risk heads to confirm the ranked list would change their audit order. Weeks 2 to 4, sign three small independent floorplan lenders or credit unions to a free retro-scan. They send 12 months of daily floored-VIN files plus their known SOT events. Report recall, false alerts per 100 dealers per week and median days of lead time over their actual discovery. Offer a free 60-day live shadow run, converting to platform plus catch fee only after at least one real catch. Also ask two audit firms for a for-cause dispatch partnership.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: SAS-paper in-house build: large lenders can do this, but independents have no analytics team, and the product adds what a conference method lacks (disposition classes, per-dealer baselines, evidence packs, dispatch capping). Vero, Solifi and other platforms analyze the lender's own payment data and have no outside-world signal, so they are integration targets or distributors (export in, module out). SBS Digital Audit, LotCount, CSI and Netresult are periodic, dealer-cooperative physical audits, and this product sends them where to go, so audit firms gain premium for-cause work and become the channel. MarketCheck is the supplier, not a rival, and licensing removes scraping ToS risk. DRN is a physical-location alternative, and MOBI is a captive-only non-commercial pilot. NextGear and Cox is the latent threat, but independent lenders that compete with NextGear are unlikely to hand their book to a Cox-owned vendor. Double-flooring stays out of scope here (it is the seed of a later cross-lender feature), so precision claims stay honest.

mutants.title: Independent Collateral Verifier for Warehouse Lenders
mutants.one_liner: Sell the same listing-vs-ledger signal not to the floorplan lender but to the lender's lender: credit funds and banks that fund floorplan and subprime auto lenders and get a borrower-supplied VIN tape they have never been able to check, delivered as a signed monthly verification certificate that borrowers pay for through facility fees.
mutants.customer: Portfolio-monitoring and credit officers at credit funds, banks and specialty-finance desks that provide warehouse or revolving lines to independent floorplan companies and subprime or BHPH auto lenders. The chooser is the warehouse lender, and the payer is usually the borrower via a monitoring fee written into the facility, the way custodian and backup-servicer fees already are. The law firms that draft these credit agreements are a second influence channel.
mutants.problem: After Tricolor and PrimaLend (Sept 2025), the lender's lender is exposed to collateral that is self-reported by the party with the strongest incentive to overstate it. It receives a VIN-level borrowing-base tape weekly or monthly. It has no auditors and no view into dealers, and field exams are annual, sample-based and weeks stale. It holds the tape but has no line of outside data to check it against. Existing floorplan-side tools are bought by the borrower, so they cannot be independent by construction.
mutants.solution: Tape-in, verification-out. The warehouse lender (or borrower on its behalf) forwards the borrowing-base tape it already receives and we return a weekly exceptions report and a signed monthly Borrowing Base Verification Certificate. (1) VIN-level reconcile of every tape VIN against listing history and the borrower's reported paydowns and collections, flagging vanished-from-listing with no paydown. (2) A borrower-level Collateral Integrity Index covering percent of tape VINs vanished-unpaid by age bucket, listing coverage ratio, and trend, benchmarked against the warehouse lender's other borrowers. (3) Because noise averages out at portfolio level, precision required is far lower than for per-VIN dispatch, and low listing coverage is reported as its own finding, not hidden. (4) Escalation: a 'for-cause exam recommended' trigger with a shortlist of dealers for a partner field-exam firm. (5) Contract language kit: a standard 'independent verification agent' covenant and fee schedule for law firms to drop into new facilities and amendments.
mutants.why_now: Sept 2025's Tricolor and PrimaLend collapses put verification failure in front of every warehouse lender and investor. Private credit funds now hold large slices of specialty-auto warehouse exposure with small monitoring teams. Facilities are being re-papered and re-underwritten, so a verification covenant can go in now instead of waiting for a renewal cycle. Cheap licensed listing history and LLM tape parsing make a weekly external check a software job instead of an exam-firm engagement.
mutants.revenue_model: Monitoring fee of about $3,000 to $6,000 per facility per month ($36k to $72k per year), paid by the borrower through the facility's fee schedule or by the lender directly, plus a $15k to $25k onboarding backtest. Add-ons include a 10 to 15 percent referral fee from partner field-exam firms on for-cause exams, and licensing the anonymized Collateral Integrity Index to ABS investors and surveillance teams. If a niche of 100 to 150 specialty-auto warehouse lenders with 3 to 5 facilities each adopts it, the ceiling is roughly 300 to 600 facilities, or $15M to $30M per year before expanding to retail-auto tapes. These figures are assumptions to test.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The funding-side buyer already owns the one input the product needs (the VIN tape) and has never had a single external data point to check it against. Verification fees are set by the chooser but paid by the borrower, who benefits from an independent stamp that supports better advance rates, so the payer wants it even when the chooser only tolerates it. Once written into facility documents, a fee line like custodian and backup servicer is sticky and renews automatically, which is a switching-cost moat that a per-dealer SaaS tool never gets.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1 to 10, list 40 warehouse lenders and credit funds active in specialty auto from trade press and deal announcements, and line up conversations with two or three finance law partners who draft these facilities. Days 10 to 30, run 10 calls with portfolio monitoring heads and offer a free one-facility 'shadow verification' using a tape they already hold. They email it, and within five business days we return a one-page findings memo covering coverage ratio, vanished-unpaid VIN count and peer benchmark. Also sign a partner field-exam firm for for-cause follow-ups. Success is one lender agreeing to a paid quarter and one law firm agreeing to circulate the covenant language.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Nothing in the competitor set sells to the funding side. Vero, Solifi, Alfa, SBS servicing and NextGear's self-audit are borrower-side tools, so a check the borrower buys from its own vendor is not independent. Cox owns NextGear, Autotrader and Dealertrack, so it is conflicted as a verifier of NextGear's rivals. CSI, LotCount, SBS Digital Audit and Netresult are dealer-level physical audits ordered by the originator, and none delivers a tape-level attestation or a peer-benchmarked index. DRN is a location signal and MOBI is a captive-only pilot. The SAS-paper method could be built by a lender, but the lender's lender lacks the daily floored data and the analytics staff, and buys instead of builds. MarketCheck is the supplier. The portfolio-level unit of analysis also neutralizes the biggest weakness of the parent (per-VIN noise).

mutants.title: Day-Zero Payoff Bridge for Floorplan Dealers
mutants.one_liner: Invert the radar: instead of catching dealers who fail to pay the floorplan lender, wire the payoff directly to the lender the day the car sells and get repaid when the retail contract funds, turning sold-out-of-trust risk into a short, fully secured receivable with data-driven underwriting.
mutants.customer: Independent and franchised dealers that sell through third-party indirect finance and get squeezed when contracts in transit, stips or unwinds stretch funding beyond the floorplan payoff window. Pilot referral partners are two or three independent floorplan lenders. Capital comes from a credit fund or family-office vehicle buying short-dated receivables. Dealer pays a per-deal fee, and the floorplan lender shares in it and saves audit cost and risk.
mutants.problem: SOT often starts as a timing gap, not fraud. The dealer has delivered the car, the retail lender has not yet funded, and the floorplan payoff clock is running. That is why honest and dishonest dealers look identical in the books for a week or more, and it is how a small cash squeeze becomes fraud. Detection tools (including the parent) only tell the lender after the timing gap has already turned into a loss or a phone call. Floorplan lenders then hold reserves and audit constantly because they cannot see the cash in transit.
mutants.solution: When a floored car sells, the dealer requests a bridge with the payoff quote, bill of sale and contract or funding-approval docs (LLM-parsed). We verify the sale with the listing signal (retail-sale signature) and cross-check the payoff quote, then wire the payoff directly to the floorplan lender, so cash never touches the dealer and cannot be diverted. We are repaid when the retail lender funds the contract, through a lockbox or deposit-account control agreement, or a notice of assignment where the retail lender allows it. The risk is receivable dilution (an unwound or charged-back contract from a creditworthy obligor), not dealer fraud. Underwriting uses obligor identity, the dealer's payoff-lag history, the dealer's unwind and chargeback record, and the listing check. Rollout runs in three phases. (1) A free dealer-side 'Unpaid VIN clock' built on the radar signal is the top of funnel and lets aged sold-not-paid VINs self-select. (2) A capped concierge bridge of up to $25k per unit. (3) Floorplan lenders name Day-Zero as an approved payoff method, in return for lower reserves and audit frequency, and receivables are sold forward to credit funds so the startup stays capital-light.
mutants.why_now: Inventory near 88 days' supply and floorplan at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps tighten dealer cash. Contracts in transit stretch a week or more. After Sky Auto Mall, lenders have less tolerance for late payoffs. Private credit is searching for short-duration, self-liquidating receivables at high gross yield. LLM document parsing plus listing signals make per-deal verification cheap enough to underwrite $150 fee deals, which was not economical with a human ops desk.
mutants.revenue_model: A fee of about 0.5 to 0.7 percent of the payoff per roughly 9-day bridge, which is about 25 percent annualized gross, plus a 10 to 20 percent referral share to the floorplan lender, capital from a credit fund at about SOFR plus 6, and the startup keeping servicing fees and a first-loss or excess-spread slice. Illustration (assumptions): a dealer bridging 15 deals a month at $22k averages about $100k outstanding and pays about $2.1k a month. 5,000 dealers at that size is roughly $500M outstanding, about $125M of gross yield and perhaps $50M to $60M net after capital cost and losses. A $99 to $199 per dealer per month clock subscription is the top-of-funnel product.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The listing-disappearance signal is too noisy to accuse a dealer but precise enough to underwrite a nine-day secured advance, because a false positive costs a declined bridge and not a false fraud allegation. Paying the floorplan lender directly makes the lender's SOT exposure structurally zero for bridged deals, so the lender is a willing distributor and co-subsidizer, and no lender integration is needed at the start because the dealer supplies the payoff quote. Detection was always a workaround for a timing mismatch that capital can simply remove.
mutants.first_30_days: Ask two independent floorplan lenders to name their 10 dealers with the most aged, late payoffs for timing reasons and to introduce us. Draft a term sheet with one credit fund or family office for a $500k to $1M pilot facility. Engage commercial-finance counsel on state licensing (some states license commercial lending and receivables purchases). Build the dealer-side Unpaid VIN clock as a landing page plus a manual crawler for the pilot dealers' sites. Aim to sign LOIs with 5 dealers and one capital source, and run the first three concierge bridges by hand to measure dilution, decline and cycle time.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: None of the parent's competitors puts capital at risk or takes payoff timing risk. Vero, Solifi, SBS, LotCount, CSI, Netresult, DRN and MOBI all police or monitor, and sell to lenders. This sells to dealers, pays lenders and shares economics with them, so it is complementary and creates no channel conflict. Audit vendors and platforms gain lower-loss books, and if lenders accept Day-Zero they need fewer audits, which is a threat to audit revenue but a benefit to lenders. NextGear and Cox is the real latent competitor because it owns floorplan plus Dealertrack contract flow, but it can serve only NextGear dealers, while independents will not send their dealers to a Cox product. The parent's research did not cover contract-in-transit funding or dealer factoring providers, so checking those incumbents is step zero. Regulatory and capital risks are the main reasons this is the highest-variance offspring.

mutants.title: Smoke Report Autopsy for Policyholder Advocates
mutants.one_liner: An adequacy auditor that scores any carrier-side smoke, ash and soot report against a public, versioned sampling grid. It then drafts the AB 1795 deficiency letter and supplemental sampling plan, and sells to public adjusters and plaintiff attorneys in the Eaton and Palisades zones.
mutants.customer: Wedge: 15-25 licensed public adjuster firms working standing-home smoke claims in Altadena, Pasadena, Pacific Palisades and Malibu, plus 3-5 plaintiff firms running the Ghazarian-style class actions against carrier-retained hygiene vendors. Later: homeowners buying direct at about $295, then carrier claims-legal teams running pre-flight audits on their own vendors.
mutants.problem: Every standing-home claimant holds a carrier-vendor IH report saying 'clean' or 'minor'. Neither the public adjuster nor the attorney can tell quickly whether it was under-sampled. Carrier-retained hygienists reportedly take about 10 samples in 3,000 sq ft, skip attics, wall cavities and HVAC, and compare results to urban background dust. A CIH second opinion costs $2k-$4k+ and takes weeks from a scarce pool. Purdue's free review is capacity-limited and does not produce claim-ready output. From Jan 1, 2027 AB 1795 makes insurers pay for testing that is 'necessary', but only if someone shows what is necessary and missing.
mutants.solution: Upload the IH report and lab PDF. LLM extraction with human QA pulls sample count, locations, media (wipe, tape lift, air, bulk), comparison basis, detection limits and skipped zones. It scores them against a public 'Adequacy Grid' built from AIHA's wildfire guide, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, 40 CFR 745.227 and 8 CCR 1529, with every criterion cited. Within 48 hours the customer gets a 2-page scorecard listing what was not sampled, a statute-cited deficiency letter for the PA or attorney to send, and a supplemental sampling plan that a partner CIH-of-record can sign, with a priced quote from a partner testing firm. The plaintiff tier ingests hundreds of reports in batch for pattern analytics (share with zero attic samples, samples per 1,000 sq ft by vendor). The grid is versioned so it re-maps when DTSC publishes standards in 2028-29. We do not sample, employ technicians, or give expert opinions.
mutants.why_now: AB 1795 was signed 9/15/2026 and takes effect 1/1/2027. It creates a 30-day inspection duty and a duty to pay for necessary testing, and it presumes smoke, ash and soot in a standing home came from the fire. Class actions over vendor sampling were filed in Feb 2026, LA County sued State Farm on 8/31/2026, and 13,000+ standing homes with smoke damage are in play. Cheap LLM document extraction makes a 48-hour, hundreds-of-dollars audit feasible where it used to be a $3k CIH engagement.
mutants.revenue_model: Public adjusters pay $395 per audit, or $2,500 a month for up to 10 active files. The CIH-signed supplemental sampling plan costs $900, split 50/50 with the partner CIH. Plaintiff-firm pattern analytics run $40k-$150k per engagement, for example a 300-report batch. The partner testing firm pays a flat referral fee on supplemental sampling it wins, or we take none if that raises fee-splitting concerns. Phase 2 sells carrier claims-legal teams a $2k-$5k per-vendor-report pre-flight audit. Bottom-up: even 15% of 13,000 homes at $395 plus a few analytics contracts is about $1.5M-$2.5M in year one, so the wedge is small and the dataset is the asset.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The unit of leverage is the omission list, not the test result. AB 1795 obliges the insurer to pay for necessary testing, and a scored list of what was not sampled and why it matters converts a fuzzy fight into a checklist the adjuster must answer in writing. Every audit also writes one structured row (vendor, square footage, samples, comparator, zones skipped), so the tool quietly builds the largest labeled dataset of how carrier vendors sample. Counter-positioning is real: HygieneTech, Rimkus and Safeguard cannot sell a tool that indicts carrier-side sampling without alienating their own clients.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: collect 25 real IH reports with consent from EFRU volunteers, two public adjusters and one attorney. Sign two CIHs at about $150/hr to review the rubric, and a toxicologist as advisor. Weeks 2-3: build Grid v0.1 as a spreadsheet plus extraction pipeline, targeting over 90% field-level accuracy on the 25 reports. Run free 48-hour audits for 10 PA files. Track whether the deficiency letter gets the carrier or FAIR Plan to authorize additional testing. Week 4: start charging $395 from audit #11, aiming for 30 paid audits and one attorney LOI for a 100-report batch pilot at about $25k. Before day 15, confirm from the chaptered AB 1795 text that there is no qualified-person or licensure rule that blocks a non-CIH from drafting a sampling plan for CIH signature.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: HygieneTech, Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup, EHS Analytical, Home BioTesting and Vert-type shops all sell sampling supply and are either carrier-conflicted or capacity-bound. We sell no sampling, so EHS and Home BioTesting become the partners who fulfil the supplemental plans and gain lead flow. Purdue's free review is bounded by grad-student capacity and has no claim-language deliverable, SLA or batch mode; we cite its method and offer a data-share and donation instead of competing. IICRC, AIHA and EFRU publish guidance and maps but sell no per-claim operational tool, so we build on them and ask EFRU for a data partnership. Safeguard's 'defensible framework' is a carrier-side essay, whereas ours is a scoring engine aimed at the policyholder side. State standards in 2028-29 change the grid's contents but not the need for an audit tool, so the business survives the standard rather than dying with it.

mutants.title: Loss-Draft Clearance Standard for Mortgage Servicers
mutants.one_liner: Mortgage servicers and portfolio lenders pay a per-loan fee for verified smoke clearance. That verification gates the final release of insurance loss-draft funds and the end of forbearance on smoke-damaged standing homes. Lenders, not carriers, become the enforcer of a defensible standard.
mutants.customer: Loss-draft and disaster-recovery departments at mortgage servicers and subservicers with concentrated Altadena, Pasadena and Palisades books, plus community banks, credit unions and CDFIs around Pasadena and the Westside. Secondary buyers: escrow and title officers on standing-home sales. Homeowners and their PAs are the delivery channel, not the payer.
mutants.problem: Servicers hold insurance proceeds on mortgaged, smoke-damaged homes and typically release them in staged draws with a final holdback against completion inspections. For destroyed homes the milestones are objective (foundation, framing). For smoke there is no completion gate: the contractor says 'cleaned', the carrier's vendor says 'clean', and the owner says the house still makes the family sick. EFRU's roughly 50 remediated homes showed 63% with elevated lead and one third with asbestos, so a lender that releases the last draw on an unverified cleaning is funding continued collateral impairment. A servicer that withholds gets complaints and unhappy borrowers paying a mortgage plus rent. I have not verified how servicers handle this today, so this is the riskiest assumption to test first.
mutants.solution: A one-page, servicer-adoptable 'Smoke Clearance Acceptance Standard' covering sampling grid, threshold basis, chain of custody and lab accreditation, tied to AB 1795, AIHA and IICRC/RIA/CIRI references and versioned for DTSC's 2028-29 standards. Alongside it, a portal where the borrower's hygienist or remediator uploads results. We verify them (automated checks plus partner CIH-of-record review) and issue a machine-readable Clearance Verification (pass, fail, or specific deficiency list) that the servicer's loss-draft workflow accepts to release the final draw or convert a forbearance. A book-level ledger shows every loan in the burn perimeter, joined to parcels, with status: not tested, tested, remediating, cleared. Testing stays paid by the insurer under AB 1795 or by the borrower from claim proceeds. The servicer pays only for verification and monitoring.
mutants.why_now: AB 1795 (effective 1/1/2027) forces insurers to pay for testing and bars ALE termination before clearance, so a verified clearance event now exists in statute and can be a lender milestone. 13,000+ standing homes with smoke damage in the LA fires, many mortgaged, are hitting the remediation and final-draw stage through 2027. Meanwhile the state standard will not exist until 2028-29, and servicers adopt vendor standards faster than agencies write them.
mutants.revenue_model: Servicers pay $250-$450 per loan verified, usually recoverable as an inspection or protective-advance line they already charge, plus $2-$5 per loan per month for ledger monitoring on flagged loans. Community banks and credit unions pay a flat $15k pilot. Hygienists and remediators can pay $50 to have their evidence pack pre-checked against the standard, since a fail costs them time. Honest sizing: LA alone is roughly 13,000 homes x about 55% mortgaged x $350 x 1.5 verifications, or about $3.7M. The business is the repeatable template for post-disaster loss-draft verification (hurricane mold, flood, wildfire) across the US, not California smoke alone.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The party with real power over whether a smoke repair is 'done' is not the carrier or the state. It is whoever holds the last check. Servicers already control disbursement, already buy standardized inspection work in bulk, and do not need to win the sampling-design argument. They need a pass/fail they can rely on. Lender incentives also align with policyholders (impaired collateral) and with carriers (fewer reopened claims and bad-faith suits), which neutralizes the parent's buyer conflict. If five servicers and credit unions accept the same evidence package, contractors and hygienists will produce to it, so the de facto standard is set by lenders.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: ask 5 public adjusters which servicers are sitting on their clients' checks, then hold 25 calls with loss-draft and disaster managers at about 10 servicers and 10 Pasadena-area banks and credit unions. The one question is what evidence would let you release the final draw on a smoke claim. Days 10-20: draft the one-page acceptance standard and get two CIHs and one toxicologist to endorse it publicly. Days 20-30: agree a paid pilot of 15-30 loans at about $300 with one credit union or servicer, and pre-check evidence packs for 10 borrowers referred by PAs. If no servicer says smoke draws are actually stuck, kill or pivot to escrow and title on resale.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: HygieneTech, Rimkus, Safeguard, EHS, Home BioTesting and Vert-type firms sell assessments to insurers and homeowners and none sells into loan servicing. They become the channel: the ones that produce evidence to our standard win a document lenders accept. Sedgwick and other carrier TPAs are structurally carrier-side, and a lender will not accept a carrier-side attestation as proof of collateral condition. The IICRC and AIHA guides and the Purdue and EFRU resources are cited inside the acceptance criteria, so they are inputs, not rivals. The state's 2028-29 standards make our criteria more specific, not obsolete, because servicers still need a verification workflow. The adjacent risk is property-preservation and loss-draft inspection vendors, who lack IH capability. We would license the standard to them white-label rather than compete.

mutants.title: Lab-Sourced Smoke Contamination Benchmark and Loss Index
mutants.one_liner: A give-to-get data cooperative that captures post-fire dust wipe, tape lift and air results directly from accredited labs, whoever ordered them. It returns percentile benchmarks to hygienists and adjusters for free, and sells the resulting contamination-prevalence and remediation-cost index to reinsurers, cat modelers, rating agencies and reserving actuaries.
mutants.customer: Payers: catastrophe and reserving actuaries at wildfire-exposed carriers, the California FAIR Plan, reinsurance brokers' analytics teams and cat-model vendors, and rating agencies. Contributors, who get the service free: IH firms, public adjusters and 2-3 AIHA-accredited environmental labs. Free-licensed users: DTSC, CDI and LA County, so the index becomes the citable reference.
mutants.problem: AB 1795 turns smoke on a standing home into a presumed covered loss with a 30-day clock, yet nobody knows contamination prevalence by distance, home age, construction, HVAC or plume. The only public dataset is EFRU's roughly 50-80 homes (63% elevated lead, one third asbestos, post-remediation). Carrier-vendor data sits in privileged silos. Cat models are built around destroyed structures, and I did not verify whether any vendor has a smoke-on-standing-homes module. Reinsurance and reserving for 2027 must price a blind tail: 13,000+ standing smoke-damage homes in LA alone, with ALE running until clearance. Every hygienist also argues about the comparison basis (urban background dust versus thresholds), and Purdue reports consultants using wrong comparators. No one has a defensible background distribution.
mutants.solution: The chokepoint is labs, not reports. Every sample, carrier-side or policyholder-side, runs through a handful of accredited labs. The co-op gives labs a differentiator: a structured electronic data deliverable plus a consent checkbox on the chain-of-custody form ('de-identified results may be contributed to the benchmark'). Contributors get a free percentile report, for example 'kitchen floor wipe lead at the 92nd percentile of 1,400 homes 0.5-1 mile from the perimeter, built 1950-79', plus a neighborhood background-dust distribution that answers the comparator fight. Buyers get a parcel-level contamination probability by contaminant, and an expected remediation-scope and cost distribution calibrated on consenting claims. Delivery is by API, CSV and annual studies, versioned, with a free license to state agencies. Public data (Cal Fire DINS, assessor year built, DTSC soil results) fills the gaps. The model generalizes to CO, OR, HI and any WUI fire.
mutants.why_now: The signing of AB 1795 on 9/15/2026 converted smoke from an adjuster judgment into a legislated, presumed, time-boxed loss. Reinsurance and carrier reserving for 2027 must now price the distribution. State standards are two to three years away and the regulators will borrow the largest population dataset available. Labs are commodity businesses hungry for differentiation, and structured data plus LLM tooling makes lab-level ingestion cheap for a small team.
mutants.revenue_model: Subscriptions of $40k-$120k a year per reinsurer, cat modeler or carrier. Bespoke reserving studies at $75k-$150k. A data-processing fee of $15-$25 per sample, paid by labs or contributors, for the percentile reports. A later licensing revenue share with cat-model vendors. Balance-sheet option once the index is trusted: a parametric smoke-remediation trigger calibrated on the co-op's data, built with a licensed MGA and reinsurer capacity. That is a 2029 step and needs admitted-carrier or surplus-lines structuring.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Everyone assumes data comes from adjudicated claims and reports. Labs are the only neutral point that sees both carrier-side and policyholder-side samples, and the percentile report solves the hygienist's biggest weakness, defending the comparison basis, so contributors have a selfish reason to opt in. The hard problem is selection bias: policyholder-side samples skew dirty, and carrier vendors sample thinly and shallowly. The co-op only earns trust if it corrects for who ordered the sample, ideally with at least one carrier's vendor data, or with a randomized sampling frame in one neighborhood. Solving that bias is the scientific moat, and it is exactly what a regulator or actuary will test first.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: pitch 3 accredited labs handling fire-zone samples on a consent-based structured feed, aiming for one signed LOI. Request EFRU's dataset and Purdue's reviewed reports under a data-sharing MOU. Days 10-20: assemble the public layer (DINS perimeters and damage inspections, assessor year built, DTSC soil data, CDI task-force figures) and publish a free 'Eaton Fire Smoke Background Dust Benchmark v0' from the EFRU sample (n of roughly 50-100) to seed usage. Days 20-30: sell two paid $15k-$25k 'Smoke Reserving Briefs' to a carrier cat or reserving team and a reinsurance-broker analytics team ahead of renewals. Sign 5 IH firms as contributors. Kill test: if no actuary will pay for a brief built on public and EFRU data, the reinsurer thesis is wrong.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: The co-op sells no assessments and writes no protocol, so HygieneTech, Rimkus, Safeguard, EHS, Home BioTesting and Vert-type firms are contributors and users of the percentile report, not rivals. None can build a neutral cross-vendor dataset because each sees only its own clients, and carrier-vendor data is privileged. EFRU holds about 50-80 homes, does not sell, and is a data partner. Purdue's guidance is method we can cite. IICRC and AIHA publish procedures rather than data. Sedgwick and other TPAs hold claim costs but not lab-grade contamination data and sit on the carrier side. The state will need the data in 2028-29 and is a licensee, not a competitor. Unlike a California-specific protocol that expires when DTSC publishes, the index gets more valuable as standards arrive, because they need a prevalence baseline.

mutants.title: Cavity ID: Tool-of-Origin Evidence via Counsel
mutants.one_liner: Expert-grade 'which tool made this part, and when' reports, built from parts the brand already holds in the US and sold through China-facing IP law firms to brands whose ex-supplier is selling their product.
mutants.customer: Wedge: branded hard-goods companies ($10M-$150M revenue: housewares, pet, fitness, hand tools, juvenile, small appliances) that sell injection-molded or die-cast products on Amazon/Walmart/Target, hold a design patent, trade dress or registered mark on the part, and ended a China supplier in the last 18 months. Buyer of record is their outside China/IP counsel (15-25 boutique cross-border firms), who engage us as a consulting expert so the work is privileged. The brand's GC or COO signs off on the disbursement.
mutants.problem: The brand sees look-alike units of its own product on Amazon, Temu and 1688 at 30% below its price, and suspects the ex-supplier is running its steel on a third shift. Today its lawyers can send a cease-and-desist built on suspicion, and the supplier answers 'that is a copy, not ours'. Marketplace takedown vendors produce screenshots and listings, not proof of which tool made the part or that it was made after the orders stopped. Without that proof the brand loses the negotiation over tool release, and losing it costs six or seven figures in tooling and margin.
mutants.solution: One product, the Tool-of-Origin Report, with no China operations and no extraction business. (1) Baseline: macro-image 30-60 retained parts per SKU, taken from the brand's own US inventory, returns and QA samples across different lots and dates. Build a cavity signature library (cavity ID marks, gate vestige, ejector-pin witness marks, parting-line and texture flaws) plus a wear-over-time curve, since tool wear is monotonic and dates the tool's state. (2) Attribution: test-buy 5-10 suspect units, match them to a cavity and tool state, and report a forensic-style likelihood ratio, including whether the tool state postdates the last PO. (3) Counsel-ready pack: chain of custody, methodology and a signed declaration from a retained independent molding-process engineer, formatted for the Amazon Report-a-Violation and APEX flows, the Alibaba IP platform, CBP recordation, a demand letter or litigation. Monitoring is bought or white-labeled from an existing vendor. Field capture in China is subcontracted, and only in a later pre-exit 'baseline while the supplier is still cooperative' tier.
mutants.why_now: The 2025 tariff whiplash and the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling (per the parent research) have produced a wave of supplier breakups. Formal-entry bulk imports rose after the end of the US de minimis exemption in 2025, which makes overrun sellers easier to reach through CBP and marketplaces. Cheap macro-imaging plus modern vision models make tool-mark statistics feasible at SMB prices, where a forensic lab used to cost $30k+ per case.
mutants.revenue_model: Baseline $4,500 per product family. Test-buy attribution report $6,500 per case (up to 10 samples). Expert declaration or testimony $350/hr through counsel. Optional 'Overrun Watch' retainer $1,500/month per family, with two attributions a year included and monitoring white-labeled. Counsel buys the report as a disbursement and marks it up under its own billing, so there are no referral fees, which avoids fee-sharing ethics problems. Target 60 clients at about $14k blended annual spend, roughly $0.85M ARR, by month 12. Gross margin about 65% (assumption). Bottom-up reachable market is roughly 1,500 qualifying brands (assumption to validate).
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The evidence a lawyer needs is not 'this is a copy'. It is 'this was made on your steel after you stopped ordering'. Tool wear is a clock: edges round, texture erodes, flash grows, and repairs leave dated marks. So parts you already own in a US warehouse from 2022, 2024 and 2025 reconstruct the wear timeline without ever visiting China. Routing the work through counsel also makes it privileged, and it moves the spend from a marketing or brand-protection budget to a legal-dispute budget that is bigger and less price-sensitive.
mutants.first_30_days: Weeks 1-2: interview 12 China-facing IP lawyers and 8 GCs, asking what evidence they wish they had at the demand-letter stage and whether they would buy at $6.5k. In parallel, run a blind validation. Buy multi-cavity molded parts from known sources across 2-3 tool states and test whether our imaging plus statistics assigns cavity and tool state correctly (target above 95%). Publish the methodology memo. Retain one independent molding-process engineer as expert of record. Weeks 3-4: sell 3 paid $2,500 Overrun Audits (test-buys plus a one-page verdict), qualified on the client owning enforceable IP on the part, through one law-firm co-marketing partner. Kill signal: fewer than 3 of 12 lawyers say they would buy, or blind accuracy below 90%.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Red Points and Corsearch detect listings and issue takedowns, and neither says which tool or supplier made a part. We sit downstream of them, buying or white-labeling their alerts, so we are not building the commoditized layer. Alitheon fingerprints individual items after enrollment and targets electronics and aerospace authentication. We do class-level cavity attribution from mold marks on ordinary consumer goods, and might license their vision stack. Harris Sliwoski and its peers give clients the DIY inventory checklist and have no evidence product, so they are the channel, not the rival. QIMA is a possible field subcontractor rather than a competitor. MoldTrax serves the molder's maintenance shop. Sourcify and freight-forwarder extraction work is dropped entirely because of its thin margins.

mutants.title: Tooling Title Diligence for Small-Brand Acquirers
mutants.one_liner: A fixed-fee, 5-day report that tells buyers of $2M-$50M product companies which molds the target legally owns, where they physically sit, and whether the factory is already selling the target's product.
mutants.customer: Buyers of physical-product brands and small manufacturers with China-made tooling: search-fund and ETA searchers, independent sponsors, lower-mid-market PE platforms and SBA 7(a) acquirers. The channel is business brokers (Quiet Light, Empire Flippers, FE International-type firms), M&A attorneys and SBA acquisition lenders. The payer is the buyer, at the LOI-to-close stage. Secondary payer is the seller, who pays for a pre-listing 'tooling-ready' file.
mutants.problem: In a small-brand acquisition the molds are the asset that everyone values at zero. The QoE accountant sees an expensed PO line, the lawyer sees a boilerplate 'all assets used in the business' rep, and the seller often cannot say whose name the tools are in or whether a bill of sale exists. If the factory holds the tools, the buyer has bought a business that the supplier can hold hostage for a 30% price hike, and the buyer also cannot move production, which matters more now that tariff rules keep changing. Nobody in the deal owns this question: brand-protection vendors sell to the brand, not to the buyer, and audit firms do not cover tooling.
mutants.solution: 'Tooling Title and Leakage Report', delivered in 5 business days. (1) Tool schedule: every tool, its location, its condition, and who holds title (bill of sale, PO language, tool-ownership clauses, supplier confirmation letters). (2) Leakage test, which is the parent's $2,500 overrun audit repurposed: buy 10 units from 1688, Alibaba, Temu and Amazon third-party sellers, and compare them with the golden sample and lot codes to say whether the supplier is already selling the product. (3) Portability score: what it would cost and how long it would take to move each tool or re-cut it, with quotes from a US or Mexican molder. (4) Deal remedies: draft closing conditions, a tool bill-of-sale assignment, custody and release agreements, and a holdback or escrow sizing suggestion for the buyer's lawyer to use. The on-site audit is optional and subcontracted, passed through at cost, and only for deals over $10M.
mutants.why_now: The searcher and ETA wave and retiring owners are pushing more small manufacturers and brands to market. The Amazon aggregator unwinding put many product brands up for resale with tooling and supplier problems. Tariff volatility (the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling per the parent research) makes 'can this brand switch factories?' a live diligence question, where in 2019 it was rarely asked. Remote marketplace scanning has become cheap enough to fit inside a fixed fee.
mutants.revenue_model: $4,900 per report, paid by the buyer, usually as a closing cost. Seller pre-listing file $2,500 through brokers. Post-close '100-day tool sovereignty plan' $12k (title cure, fingerprint baseline, second-source quotes). Portfolio monitoring for PE sponsors $2,000/month per physical-product company. Model: 240 reports a year at month 12 is about $1.2M, plus a 25% attach rate on the plan (60 plans at $12k) is about $0.7M. Reachable market is assumed at roughly 1,500 physical-product deals a year, to be validated with brokers. Lenders or brokers might pay for reports on deals that later close.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: This is the same asset as the parent idea, but a far better moment to sell it. A breakup victim only hires you once they are already hurt and have already lost leverage. An acquirer is at peak willingness to pay, because they are about to wire $5M, and the report's cost is rounding error on the deal. The finding also turns straight into money: a missing bill of sale becomes a closing condition, a holdback or a price cut. A short-lived supplier concentration risk becomes a negotiating chip. Diligence is also the top of a repeat-customer funnel, since a sponsor with 6 platform companies buys monitoring on all of them.
mutants.first_30_days: Build a redacted sample report from public listings and a mock data room. Pitch 6 brokers and 3 searcher communities, offering 3 free reports on live deals, in exchange for testimonials and a written referral agreement, since a diligence step that reduces buyer fear helps brokers close deals. Then sell 5 paid reports at an introductory $3,500. Get one M&A attorney to endorse the closing-condition language. Line up two China audit contractors by referral for the on-site option. Kill signal: brokers refuse to introduce the report to buyers, or no buyer will pay $3.5k.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Red Points and Corsearch sell takedown subscriptions to brands and have no deal-time product for a buyer or a lender. QIMA runs supplier audits without tooling-title verification, and is too slow and costly for a $3M deal, so it becomes a subcontractor for large deals. Harris Sliwoski sells legal hours after a dispute, so we are the fact base their M&A-side peers lack. Alitheon and MoldTrax do not play in deal timelines. Sourcify is a natural post-close channel for the re-sourcing step. Accounting-based QoE and general legal diligence firms are the real adjacent substitutes, and they do not physically verify tools or test the marketplace (assumption, to check in the 20 first conversations).

mutants.title: Tool Passport: Molds That Report Themselves
mutants.one_liner: An OEM-owned, tamper-evident magnetic cycle counter and registry that makes every mold or die report its own location and shot count, so an unauthorized overrun shows up on the owner's screen and, in time, verified tools can be financed and insured.
mutants.customer: Wedge: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50M-$500M) that have just moved, or are moving, tools out of China to US, Mexican, Vietnamese or Indian molders and never want a second breakup. Second user: the receiving nearshore molder, who installs the tag to earn 'verified' status with skittish customers. Later payers: tooling lenders, insurers and procurement teams that require a Passport.
mutants.problem: Even after reshoring, the OEM's tools sit in someone else's building with no independent record of how many shots they have run, on which press or when. The molder's own counters and MES data are self-reported. Enforcement is all after-the-fact forensics, which is expensive and easy to dispute. Because tools cannot be verified, they are worth nothing as collateral, cannot be insured on custody, and force OEMs into blunt contracts with minimum order quantities and amortization games.
mutants.solution: Phase 1 product, 'Tool Heartbeat', is a magnet-mount IP67 tag with an accelerometer that counts mold-open and mold-close cycles from vibration signatures, geofences the tool, detects removal, stores and forwards data over LTE-M, and reports to a per-tool 'passport': QR plate, serial, photo and fingerprint baseline, custody chain, shot ledger versus POs. Silence is contractually a breach. A model 'Tool Passport Addendum' for MSAs, drafted with a China-facing law firm, gives the OEM tag access and audit rights. Phase 2 uses the ledger as the meter for pay-per-shot billing and escrow, so the molder is paid per verified shot and proves innocence. Phase 3 is the registry as a standard: a VIN-and-Carfax for tools that lenders accept for collateral and underwriters use for custody cover. Phase 4 is Passport-backed tooling finance and custody insurance, where the balance-sheet upside sits. Tools still in China get the Census-and-forensics service from the parent, not tags, until SIM roaming and consent barriers are solved.
mutants.why_now: Reshoring has created thousands of just-moved tools whose owners are motivated to prevent a repeat. LTE-M and NB-IoT modules with IMUs now cost roughly $25-45 in BOM for a 3-5 year tag. EUROMAP 77 / OPC UA 40077 machine interfaces make molder-side data available to cross-check the independent witness. The tariff-driven wave of moves in 2025-26 (per the parent research) means a stock of new supplier relationships where the tag can be built into the contract from day one.
mutants.revenue_model: Hardware $150 per tag (roughly 60% margin at scale), $10 per tool per month for the ledger and alerts, and $1,000 per site onboarding (QR plates, fingerprint baseline, custody paperwork). A 60-tool OEM pays about $22k in year one and $7k a year after. Reaching $1M ARR takes about 140 OEM-sites, so the early business is small. The upside is in the standard: verified-tool finance fees and custody insurance premiums, plus a 'Passport Verified' seal for molders. This is a longer-dated bet, and the near-term money rests on services and hardware.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The parent asks how to prove theft afterward. The inversion is that a tool is the only expensive asset in manufacturing that reports nothing about itself. A cycle count is a signal the tool already produces every 30 seconds through its own vibration, and no one owns it as a customer-side record. Once an independent meter exists, the honest molder benefits as much as the OEM, because it settles quantity disputes, proves clean custody and lets the molder offer pay-per-shot pricing. That aligned incentive is what makes a standard plausible, where a policing tool would not spread.
mutants.first_30_days: Weeks 1-3: build 10 prototype tags from an off-the-shelf LTE-M module and IMU (Blues Notecard-class) in a magnetic housing, about $3k. Validate cycle-count accuracy (target within 1%) on 2-3 presses at a friendly Ohio molder who gets free tags and 'Passport-ready' status. Weeks 2-4: pre-sell 3 OEM pilots at $2,400 for 10 tags plus a year of service with a refundable deposit, using the Reshoring Initiative and Ohio plant-manager networks. Draft the Addendum with one law firm. Use the $2,500 Marketplace Overrun Audit as the top-of-funnel cross-sell. Kill signal: vibration counting cannot reach 98% accuracy across press types, or fewer than 2 of 10 OEMs will sign a pilot.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Red Points and Corsearch operate on marketplaces after products have shipped. We work at the tool and stop overruns being made unseen, and we can hand them evidence. Alitheon authenticates individual items and has no way to know a tool's shot count or location, so their tech becomes a possible fingerprint tier. Harris Sliwoski tells clients to put permanent asset IDs on tools and audit quarterly. We productize that checklist into a continuous witness, and they are the natural channel for the Addendum. QIMA does periodic audits, so it becomes the install and spot-check subcontractor. MoldTrax and mold shot counters serve the molder's maintenance shop with self-reported data, while ours is customer-owned, independent and tamper-evident (whether other OEM-side products exist is unverified). Sourcify and sourcing agents are a channel, because provable custody helps their nearshore programs.

mutants.title: Recall Drills: State QC Findings Become Worker Training
mutants.one_liner: A recall-notice system for SNAP errors: every finding from a state's own QC review and every H.R.1 rule change becomes a dollar-tagged synthetic drill within 14 days, delivered through the state's CQI field staff to new hires in its highest-error counties, with an audit trail for corrective-action plans.
mutants.customer: Wedge: North Carolina's SNAP continuous-quality-improvement (CQI) unit. Its staff are former county workers who visit each of the 100 county departments monthly, plus the counties the state has already flagged as high-error. NC's 6.69% rate sits 0.69 points above the 6% cliff, and the parent research puts crossing it at about $140M a year. Payer: the state SNAP director's training/CQI line. Users: CQI specialists and county supervisors. Next states: Louisiana (7.61%) and any state within about 1.5 points of a 6/8/10% tier line.
mutants.problem: QC findings reach workers months after the case action, as webinars and memos. H.R.1 rule churn (work-requirement, noncitizen and utility-allowance changes) creates fresh errors faster than classroom training absorbs them. New hires learn on live caseloads, and Kansas cites turnover as an error driver. Counties are told 'documenting, documenting, documenting' but have no per-worker evidence trail. A handful of CQI staff cannot be in 100 counties every day.
mutants.solution: Three pieces. (1) An error-to-drill pipeline: CQI staff upload a QC finding at element level (stacked shelter deduction after a rent change, biweekly pay-stub conversion, household member who left). Within 14 days we return a synthetic twin case, scored with PolicyEngine as the oracle and hand-checked against the state manual, and push it to the assigned counties. (2) A 30-day new-hire certification track over the top three error elements, with pre/post scores and time-to-competency. (3) A CQI console with per-county and per-worker error-type heatmaps and a one-click 'CAP evidence packet' PDF (assigned, completed, score trend) that counties attach to corrective-action documentation. Drills test the input and verification decisions workers actually make (what to verify, which income to budget, which old entry to close), not the arithmetic the eligibility system already does.
mutants.why_now: The FY2027 QC sample year opens Oct 1, 2026. It is the first year measured under the new rules and it sets the FY2030 cost share (FY2029 and later use the rate from three fiscal years earlier). FY2028 exposure is effectively locked to the state's better of FY2025 or FY2026, so the next lever is FY2027 onward. The 75% state/local admin cost share also starts Oct 1, 2026. USDA published FY2025 rates on June 24, 2026: 41 states are above 6% and the national rate is 10.62%, and states above 6% must file remediation plans. States are visibly buying: Alabama DHR posted a QC assessment and training RFP, and NC's one-click 'close old deduction' prompt has been used more than 20,000 times, which shows targeted micro-interventions get adopted.
mutants.revenue_model: Year-1 state pilot of $60-90k for 12-15 named counties (verify it sits under each state's small-purchase limit). This expands to statewide at $250-400k a year. Counties outside the state contract pay $150-300 per worker, and new-hire certification is $250 per hire. All prices are unvalidated, so get the budget line from the CQI director before writing case #13. Realistic ceiling is about $10-20M ARR across the roughly 40 states above the threshold, so this is the modest-ceiling, fast-to-cash version.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The product is closing the lag, not teaching skill. States already hold the scarcest asset, their own QC findings, and lose months turning it into training. A recall loop (finding, twin drill, completion evidence) cannot be copied by a vendor that only has the generic USDA taxonomy. It is one data-sharing MOU with a state QC unit away, and US Digital Response reports such agreements take 3 weeks to 3 months. Pick the launch state by distance to a cliff times benefit dollars, not by pain: NY at 13% needs a 3-point cut just to reach the 10% tier, while NC at 6.69% can plausibly cross 6%. A 0%-error county is still charged for the state average, so the state CQI unit, not the county, is the customer.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-7: 20 calls with NC CQI staff, county DSS directors and the state county association, asking who owns a budget line for this and what the last training tool cost. Days 5-15: build 12 drills from public sources only (H.R.1 rule changes, the publicly described stacked-shelter-deduction failure, biweekly wage conversion, household-member removal), and script the 14-day finding-to-drill workflow. Days 15-25: run a 3-county new-hire pre/post pilot with CQI staff as co-facilitators. Days 25-30: hand the state a CAP evidence packet sample and a one-page letter of intent with a price, and ask the CQI director to name the budget line.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Maximus Accuracy Assistant flags risk inside the live workflow and does not train. We use the same error patterns upstream and can pass them to Maximus, so it is a channel or acquirer, not a rival. State academies and NC's monthly QC webinars are free supply, but they are lecture-style with no per-worker measurement. We arm the CQI staff who run them and produce evidence they cannot. Code for America and PolicyEngine are flow and rules tools. PolicyEngine is a commodity input to our scoring, and the moat is the state's own finding library plus the audit trail. Kognito sold soft-skill simulations with no dollar metric. Every drill here is tagged to a QC element and its cost-share exposure. PCG, PSI and Deloitte sell consultant hours, while this is a persistent loop and evidence record priced below a single consultant week.

mutants.title: Federal-Agreement Lab for State SNAP QC Reviewers
mutants.one_liner: Sell calibration drills to the small, high-leverage group whose findings set the official error rate, the state QC reviewers, scoring them against a federal answer key and putting part of the fee at risk on the state-federal disagreement rate.
mutants.customer: State SNAP Quality Control unit directors and the state SNAP directors who sponsor them, in the 41 states above 6% that must now file remediation plans. Each QC unit is a few dozen reviewers. Warm lead: Alabama DHR, which posted an RFP for 'SNAP Quality Control review assessment and training'. Check who won and at what scope. Targets: states within about 1 point of a tier line, once the FY2025 state table is pulled.
mutants.problem: The official rate is not the state's own number. USDA re-reviews a subsample and adjusts (regresses) the state's findings, and disputed differences go to arbitration. Rates are cliffs (6/8/10%), each worth tens to hundreds of millions in state benefit cost. A state QC reviewer who under-calls errors gets corrected upward by federal re-review. One who over-calls inflates the state's own rate. QC units are small and turnover-prone, and the FNS 310 handbook is dense. Today that calibration happens ad hoc, in meetings or through occasional consultants.
mutants.solution: A library of about 200 synthetic completed-review packets: case file, interview notes and an 'as-reviewed' finding, with planted misses and planted false alarms. Answer keys are adjudicated by retired FNS and state reviewers and cite FNS 310 sections. Reviewers find the errors, and we score agreement with the key by element (income, household composition, shelter, resources, ABAWD/H.R.1 rules), by reviewer and by supervisor. We add weekly live calibration sessions run by the retired reviewers, and an arbitration-readiness checklist. We do not perform QC reviews. We train and score, which keeps us clear of the federal oversight rules for third-party QC contractors (verify against the 2018 Farm Bill provisions). Method is symmetric: the goal is agreement with the federal standard, not lower error counts.
mutants.why_now: FY2025 rates came out June 24, 2026: 41 states above 6% and a 10.62% national rate. FY2026 rates finalize through federal re-review and arbitration into mid-2027, and states can use the better of FY2025 and FY2026 for FY2028. The FY2027 sample opens Oct 1, 2026 and sets FY2030 cost share. H.R.1 made every QC finding a budget line, so QC directors now have executive attention and remediation-plan deadlines. The Alabama RFP shows states already buy QC-side assessment and training.
mutants.revenue_model: $90-250k per state QC unit per year: about $2.5-4k per reviewer seat, a packet-library license and quarterly calibration sessions. 20-25% of the fee is at risk, refunded if the state-federal difference rate on FNS re-reviewed cases does not narrow. FNS measures that outcome, not us. 41 states at 40% penetration is about $5-8M ARR, so the ceiling is small but each logo is high-value and fast to close. Expansion: Medicaid eligibility-error programs (H.R.1 adds payment reductions starting around FY2030, verify), plus a per-case add-on for arbitration memo review. Prices are unvalidated assumptions.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Dollars at stake per trained head is 100-1000x higher for QC reviewers than for eligibility workers. A 30-person unit's calibration can swing a tier cliff worth $100M+, and a county worker's cannot. The regressed rate turns under-calling into a hidden tax, not good luck. Unlike eligibility policy, which varies by state, QC review method is national (FNS 310), so one packet library serves every state. That fixes the parent's per-state case-library cost problem. The buyer population is tiny, homogeneous and reachable through a few networks.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-5: pull the Alabama RFP, announcement and results documents to learn the winner, scope and price. Recruit 2 retired state or FNS QC reviewers as adjudicators at $100-150 an hour. Days 5-18: write 25 planted-error packets from the public FNS 310 handbook and published arbitration guidance. Days 10-30: reach 15 QC directors through APHSA payment-accuracy contacts and FNS regional liaisons. Offer a free blind 10-packet test for 5 of their reviewers and return an agreement-gap report within a week. Convert 1-2 to $25-40k pilots via simplified procurement.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Maximus Accuracy Assistant works before issuance on eligibility workers' cases, and QC reviewers are not its user. State academies and webinars teach eligibility policy and cannot score reviewer agreement with a federal key. PCG, Policy Studies and similar consultancies sell engagement hours on reviews and corrective-action plans. We do no reviews, so we avoid the contractor-oversight burden and the conflict of grading our own work (verify), and we cost a fraction of a consultancy engagement. Code for America and PolicyEngine are flow and rules tools with no review-standard content. Kognito-style simulation had no dollar-weighted outcome or federal answer key. The Alabama RFP winner is the one real competitor to profile in week one.

mutants.title: Unit Tests for Benefit Law: Eligibility System Conformance
mutants.one_liner: Invert the drill: aim the same synthetic households and adjudicated answer keys at the eligibility software itself, selling H.R.1 conformance test packs to states and system vendors, with an aim to become the standard test suite that state RFPs cite.

mutants.solution: H.R.1 Conformance Pack v1: about 250 synthetic households aimed at the edges of each changed rule (income at the threshold, mixed-status households, month-boundary changes, shelter and utility interactions), each with an expected outcome and a citation trail to statute, USDA guidance and the state manual. The state's own policy staff sign off the answer key, so we test state policy against state system and do not have to settle federal ambiguity. Where state policy and federal guidance conflict, we flag it as a second deliverable, a QC-risk memo. Delivery fits existing UAT: scenario scripts and machine-readable fixtures with expected results, plus a divergence report. Later: a regression subscription refreshed on every guidance change, vendor pre-certification, and household-level evaluation sets for AI intake and caseworker-assist tools.
mutants.why_now: Every state must change its SNAP and Medicaid eligibility logic within months of each other, and Medicaid work requirements and six-month renewals land around Jan 2027. AI tools are entering benefits workflows and agencies have no household-level ground truth to test them against. USDA's FY2025 numbers (41 states above 6%, 10.62% nationally) make a systemic logic bug politically and financially radioactive. Open-source rules engines (PolicyEngine) and LLM-assisted drafting cut the cost of building cases, so adjudication, not authoring, is now the scarce step.
mutants.revenue_model: Per-state pack at $40-120k per major rule change, and a regression subscription at $100-250k a year per program per state. Vendor certification runs at $15-50k and AI-tool evaluation runs at $10-30k. Bottom-up: 50 states x 3 programs x about $300k, so $30-60M ARR is a plausible ceiling, and more if state RFPs cite the suite as an acceptance criterion. Much of the spend can draw federal IT matching funds in system-change budgets (verify per program). Prices are unvalidated assumptions.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Independence is the product, in the way UL or a ratings agency is. Vendors cannot credibly grade their own homework, and states cannot staff independent test authorship, so the cornered resource is the adjudicated, state-signed answer key: expert time that compounds across states and rule changes. Testing the machine reaches a bigger error source than training people, and the same answer-key corpus later powers worker drills, QC calibration and AI evaluation. A standard is reachable because states already buy test scripts and would rather cite a neutral suite than write their own.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick 12 H.R.1 SNAP provisions from USDA implementation memos and write 60 boundary-case households. Run them through PolicyEngine and through 2-3 states' public online benefit screeners, which needs no system access. Days 10-18: send each state policy director a private divergence report with 3-5 mismatches and an offer of the full pack. Days 15-30: sign 1-2 paid $25-40k UAT-pack pilots with a state policy or IT lead, and start talks with a system integrator's state account team about pre-certification. Recruit 2 ex-state policy and ex-FNS adjudicators to sign keys.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Maximus Accuracy Assistant scores live cases for risk and does not test system logic. Code for America and Nava help states build and communicate rules, not produce independent conformance suites. PolicyEngine is the natural supplier and partner (open-source engine, nonprofit, no state-signed answer keys or sales motion), and its SNAP screener validation is not a state-system acceptance test. Vals AI's Public Benefits Bench (with Code for America and the Center for Civic Futures) is a proprietary question-answering benchmark for beneficiary inquiries. It does not test household eligibility or benefit calculations, so we supply the household-level layer and could partner. System vendors and IV&V firms test their own or generic project deliverables, and independence is our counter-position. The Kognito failure is irrelevant here because the buyer is a funded IT/UAT process, not a training budget. State academies are not substitutes.

mutants.title: Site-Control Check for Utility Large-Load Queues
mutants.one_liner: A neutral 48-hour report on whether each large-load applicant really controls the land it names, sold to the utilities that must now screen speculative data center requests and billed through to the applicants.
mutants.customer: Large-load and interconnection managers, plus regulatory counsel, at G&T electric co-ops, municipal utilities and mid-size wires companies. Wedge: Texas co-ops, munis and mid-size TDUs (about 150 entities), then SPP and MISO states. The buyer is the utility. The applicant pays through the study-fee schedule.
mutants.problem: Utilities are buried in large-load requests, and many are speculative. The same parcel is shopped to several utilities. 'Site control' is often an applicant-supplied PDF or a non-binding LOI. The utility has to decide which requests get $100k+ studies and reserved capacity. A wrong guess strands capital or pushes cost onto ratepayers. Regulators and commissions now expect screening, but staff have no independent way to check control of land beyond what the applicant says.
mutants.solution:
The utility requires the applicant to list its parcels, and we do the rest.
1. Pull recorded instruments on those parcels and their neighbors from county portals, targeted per parcel with a landman fallback, so no bulk licence is needed.
2. Classify by reading the image rather than the clerk's label, and resolve the LLC family by notary, return-to firm and address.
3. Deliver a one-page Site-Control Report graded Recorded, Partial, Unrecorded or Conflicting. It shows acreage under recorded control against the acreage the claimed MW implies, option expiry dates, competing claimants, and duplicate-request flags across utilities through an opt-in hashed-parcel index.
4. Upsell a monthly territory sweep, which is the original Courthouse Tape, for assemblies that have not filed a request yet.
A human landman reviews every Partial or Conflicting result.
mutants.why_now: Utilities are being pushed to prove large-load requests are real. Texas SB 6 (2025) reportedly requires 75 MW+ applicants to show site control, disclose duplicate requests and pay study fees. Other utilities have added financial-commitment tariffs. ERCOT's large-load queue is reported at well over 200 GW, far beyond any buildable amount. LLM vision now reads messy recorded instruments accurately. FinCEN's exemption of domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. Verify the SB 6 details before quoting them to customers.
mutants.revenue_model: $1,500-$3,000 per Site-Control Report, added as a pass-through line to the applicant's study-fee schedule. $60k-$150k a year per utility for the territory sweep, unlimited reports and a regulator-ready audit pack. Bottom-up: 60 utilities at about $80k is $4.8M ARR in Texas and neighboring states. 500 utilities nationally is about $40M ARR. Later add-on: applicants buy a neutral verified-site-control certificate to speed their queue position.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Verification is much easier than detection. Because the utility can compel the parcel list, we skip the hardest parts of the parent: not knowing where to look, statewide bulk scraping, and false positives. A missing or unrecorded instrument becomes a finding in its own right, which also dodges the doubt that developers may not record option memos before announcement. Only a utility-side neutral can build the moat. Developers shop the same parcel to many utilities, and no utility will share its queue with a vendor that also sells to developers. A cross-utility duplicate-parcel index is therefore a network effect that Enverus or Paces cannot build without losing the trust of their own developer customers.
mutants.first_30_days: Take Texas. Call 25 co-op and muni large-load contacts through the Texas Electric Cooperatives and Texas Public Power Association networks and the NRECA circuit. Offer a free retrospective audit of each utility's last 10 requests using only recorded instruments. Report what share had no recorded control, duplicate claims or expired options. Convert two utilities to $20k-$30k paid pilots on new requests. In parallel, confirm which county portals allow per-parcel commercial retrieval and line up two landmen for offline counties.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Every competitor in the research sells to developers or investors. Enverus, Paces, GridCARE and DC Byte help a developer find or defend its own site, so utilities cannot treat them as neutral verifiers of a developer's claim. Cleanview and Heatmap Pro start at permit or news, which is after the queue decision. ATTOM, Regrid and Reonomy sell deeds and LLC piercing but not options, leases or easements, and do no per-request verification. Pandell manages a client's own documents. We sell only to the utility side, never to developers, and the audit trail suits a regulator. The remaining risk is Enverus adding the feature, so the cross-utility index and utility trust are the defence.

mutants.title: Holdout Ledger: Landowner-Side Assembly Intelligence
mutants.one_liner: The landowner's half of the courthouse tape. It shows farm families and heirs in an assembly corridor who is buying around them, how close the buyer is to finishing, and how much leverage the last holdouts have, paid on closing.
mutants.customer: Owners of 100-2,000 acres in counties where recorded options and easements cluster, reached through ag and land-use attorneys, county farm bureaus, rural lenders and direct mail. Wedge: heirs, tenants-in-common and absentee owners who get anonymous offers under NDA. The payer is the landowner, on a contingent fee, plus subscribing law firms.
mutants.problem: Each landowner is approached alone by a landman working for an anonymous LLC. NDAs stop neighbors comparing notes. The developer sees the whole assembly and the owner sees one offer. Owners sign early and cheap, or hold out blindly, and cannot tell whether their parcel is a keystone or an afterthought. Landmen work for the buyer, local lawyers rarely have county-wide data, and county officials learn of the project from a leaked story.
mutants.solution:
1. 'Neighbor Check': enter a parcel or address and get a map of recorded instruments within about 5 miles, classified from the image. It shows the LLC family behind them, the share of the plausible footprint already recorded, whether the parcel sits on a critical path (contiguity, road access, a line crossing), expiring options, and a plain-English read of what the pattern usually means.
2. Owners in a cluster can opt into a negotiating pool, like the mineral-owner associations in oil and gas leasing. A licensed land broker or attorney partner represents them. We supply the analytics and take a success fee on closing.
3. We sell a group map subscription to ag and land-use law firms and farm-bureau chapters.
mutants.why_now: The 2025-26 large-load land rush has put anonymous NDA'd offers in front of thousands of rural owners, and local fights over data center land deals are widely reported. Owners can now see the buyer's footprint because public recorded memoranda can be read at scale with LLM vision. FinCEN's exemption for domestic companies means owners cannot ask who is behind the LLC and get a federal answer, so primary records are the only route. Reported prices such as roughly $100k an acre offered near Hill County, Texas, make the information gap worth real money to owners.
mutants.revenue_model: Free lookup as lead generation. $149-$399 for a full parcel report. A contingent success fee of 1.5%-3% of total consideration at closing, collected through a licensed broker affiliate. Example: a 300-acre owner closing a $4M option-plus-lease package yields $60k-$120k. $300-$800 a month per law firm or farm-bureau seat. Ten closed deals in year one is roughly $500k-$1M, at very low marginal cost after the data pull.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The developer's own recorded memoranda reveal how complete the assembly is, and holdout value peaks in the last 20-30% of parcels. That is the moment owners are least informed. Every existing vendor's paying customer is the developer, so none can serve the counterparty without alienating buyers. That is counter-positioning in Helmer's sense. Landowners are numerous, each needs the service once, and assessor rolls are public, so mail reaches them cheaply. The demand is one-shot and high-stakes, which suits a contingent fee better than SaaS. The data burden is also small: a few dozen instruments per cluster, pulled per parcel, with none of the statewide bulk-ingestion risk.
mutants.first_30_days: Pick one county with a visible assembly. The parent's method of pulling 24 months of instruments gives the pattern. Mail 400 landowners within the cluster a letter with a QR code: 'Three LLCs using the same law firm recorded options on X acres within 4 miles of your land.' Offer a free Neighbor Check, then a $199 report. Sign a referral and co-marketing agreement with one licensed land broker and one ag attorney. Get 5 owners into a pooled negotiation and 20 paid reports. Before launch, have counsel confirm the broker-licensing and fee-sharing rules in the state (lawyers generally cannot split fees with non-lawyers), and use only public records. We are never a party to any NDA.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: ATTOM, Regrid, Reonomy, PropertyRadar, Enverus, Paces, Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, GridCARE and Pandell all sell to developers, investors, utilities or the trade. None serves the seller, and none could do so without conflicting with its own customers. Generic land brokerages sell listings but do not read recorded non-deed instruments or unmask LLC families. Landman firms work for the buyer. Nothing in the research offers owners a cluster map or holdout-leverage view. The bulk-access risk is avoided because the work is targeted, parcel by parcel, within a county already showing activity. Weaknesses: a developer or its counsel may push back, some states restrict non-lawyer negotiation help, and reputation matters in small communities.

mutants.title: Recorder Rails: County-Funded Clean Index of Instruments
mutants.one_liner: AI re-indexing and compliance scans that counties buy from their own records-modernization funds. In return we hold the cleaned, entity-resolved index of every non-deed instrument, which becomes the data layer for assembly alerts and much else.
mutants.customer: County recorders and clerks (about 3,100 counties), who pay first, starting with mid-size rural and exurban counties in data-center and energy corridors where economic development offices also want the assembly view. Downstream buyers are the parent's developers, utilities and funds, plus ag lenders and title-adjacent firms.
mutants.problem: The parent's product depends on county-by-county recorder access and on document types that are often wrong ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'Agreement'). Ingestion is a grind, bulk commercial-use rules vary, and the good data is scattered. Counties have their own pains: aging archives, mandated redaction of sensitive data, covenant-review requests and property-fraud pressure, all with thin staff.
