They already spend on indexing and digitization from earmarked funds. Nobody owns a clean cross-county index of non-deed instruments.
mutants.solution:
1. Sell the county a fixed-price Hidden Instruments Audit. AI reclassifies its mislabeled and 'Other' instruments from the images, corrects grantor and grantee indexing, flags sensitive-data and statutory items such as discriminatory covenants, and gives the county a corrected index and an economic-development view of large instruments.
2. In the agreement, the county gives bulk access to the images and index at cost, and we keep the right to publish the derived classification and entity graph. The underlying records are already public.
3. Publish an open taxonomy for non-deed instruments, in the manner of MISMO for mortgages, so counties and vendors can adopt it.
4. Keep the labeled corpus and the LLC-family graph proprietary and build products on it: Courthouse Tape alerts, the utility site-control check, landowner tools, alt-data licences and collateral-encumbrance alerts for ag lenders.
mutants.why_now: LLM vision has collapsed the cost of reading a scanned page, so a re-index that once cost a labor-intensive vendor per-page fees is now cheap. Counties are under fresh mandates to review archives: covenant-removal laws in a number of states, and reportedly some large counties have already run AI covenant scans (verify which). Property-fraud concern is high. FinCEN's exemption of domestic companies from beneficial-ownership reporting makes primary-record entity resolution more valuable. The large-load land rush gives the resulting index an immediate paying use. Rural counties facing data center proposals want visibility into assembly.
mutants.revenue_model: County audits at $9k-$40k per county, fitted under small-purchase thresholds and paid from records-modernization or technology funds, then $5k-$20k a year to maintain. Data licences to funds at $50k-$150k a year. Downstream product revenue per the parent: developer or utility seats at $2k-$8k a month and title packets at $750-$2,000. A plausible year-three target is 300 counties at about $25k, or $7.5M, plus $5M-$10M of licences and subscriptions. Gross margin on data products should exceed 70% once ingestion is standardized.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is county cooperation, not the classifier. So invert who pays. Instead of buying access from counties, we get paid by them to solve a problem they already fund, and the by-product is the corpus. A county that gets a corrected index and a free economic-development dashboard has little reason to block a downstream data feed, and other counties will copy the arrangement. This is a cornered resource plus switching costs that build county by county. Incumbents face asymmetry: indexing and digitization vendors earn from labor-based per-page work, so AI re-indexing at a fraction of the price undercuts their own revenue. Title plants index for title, not for cross-county assembly detection.
mutants.first_30_days: Run an offline proof on two rumored-project counties. Pull 24 months of instruments, reclassify 'Other' and 'Agreement' filings, and count how many option memoranda were recorded before the announcement. If that count is low, shift the wedge to easement and transmission detection. Show each recorder the result: 'We found N large instruments mislabeled as Other.' Offer a $9,500 audit to three counties, and separately sell the free 'who is assembling where' memo to 10 site-selection consultants to fund the corpus. Check each state's rules on commercial use of bulk records and on data-sharing agreements, and get county counsel comfortable.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: The parent's competitors are adjacent data sellers: ATTOM, Regrid and Reonomy sell deeds, mortgages and parcels; Enverus, Paces and GridCARE serve a client's own site; Cleanview, DC Byte and Heatmap Pro start after permits or news; Pandell manages a client's own documents. None of them controls the recorder relationship. Title plants such as First American DataTree hold indexed documents for title workflows, not a cleaned cross-county alert feed. The county-software and digitization vendors (Tyler, Fidlar and Kofile appear to be the main ones, none verified here) are the real risk and might build the same thing. We differ by working on top of whichever system the county runs, by contracting with the county rather than the vendor, and by owning the entity graph. Enverus can add a feature but not a hundred county contracts.

mutants.title: Ship-Date Cliff Audits for Phased Campuses
mutants.one_liner: A fixed-fee clock-map, rider-negotiation and proof-test sprint for developers of multi-phase data center campuses whose pre-bought gensets, UPS and chillers were shipped long before the halls they serve, so the OEM 18-months-from-ship outer limit expires before startup.
mutants.customer: Wedge buyer: the VP of procurement or construction director at colo developers and neoclouds building multi-phase campuses (100MW+, with phases 2-4 not yet energized) that accepted long-lead MEP deliveries ahead of the shell. Start with generators, then UPS. Secondary buyer: the lender's technical advisor asking for an equipment warranty schedule at draw or refinancing.
mutants.problem: The judges and the competitor check both found that the parent's premise is too broad. Startup plus load-bank IST already loads most equipment, so the 'idle hall' exposure is narrow. The clean exposure is different. OEM terms run to the earlier of about 12 months from startup or 18 months from factory ship (Cummins, Eaton and Trane terms in the research). Developers buy gear in blocks for phases 2-4 to lock lead-time slots and pre-tariff prices, and take delivery into yards or spare rooms. When a phase slips, the outer limit lapses before the unit is ever started. Storage voiding conditions (heaters, battery freshening charges, engine exercise) are usually undocumented, so an OEM can also deny on those grounds. Procurement has moved on, the ship date lives in a bill of lading nobody rereads, and ops inherits the unit with no idea the clock ran out.
mutants.solution: 1) Cliff calendar. Per serial number, extract ship date (bill of lading, delivery ticket), planned startup, outer-limit date and voiding conditions. The LLM pipeline is an internal tool; the deliverable is a one-page dated list of cliffs. 2) Rider sprint. Before each cliff, negotiate a written start-date deferral or delayed-start rider with the OEM. Package it campus-wide, because the owner's phase 3-4 orders are the leverage a single-unit rider buyer lacks. 3) Storage-compliance repair. Fix missing exercise, heater and battery-charge logs so the OEM loses its easy denial grounds. 4) Proof test. For installed units 6-9 months before the cliff, run a staged load test using a load-bank rental partner, then file claims with OEM-grade evidence while the OEM is still liable. Contingency is not the lead model.
mutants.why_now: Long-lead power gear (gensets, transformers, switchgear) is being bought years ahead of buildings, and phase slippage is widespread in 2026 reporting. Tariffs make each unit more expensive, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. LLMs make serial-level extraction from delivery documents cheap. Delayed-start riders exist (Trane), so the ask is normal to OEMs but rarely made.
mutants.revenue_model: $30-60K fixed fee per campus phase for the cliff calendar plus rider negotiation. $60-120K per year campus retainer that keeps the calendar live as phases progress. Load-test pass-through with a 15% markup, plus a referral fee from the rental partner. Success fee of 20% of OEM-accepted claim value, measured by the OEM's claim number or credit memo, and 10% of the discount won on riders versus list. Assumption to validate: about 30 campus programs at roughly $80K per year is about $2.4M ARR with 2-3 people.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The exposed population is defined by shipment date versus startup date, not by whether a hall is idle. That makes it provable from documents and public filings before any owner talks to you. It also makes the contingency-collection problem disappear: a signed deferral or an OEM credit memo is a countable outcome, unlike 'avoided repair cost'. The leverage is future orders across the campus, which the owner has and a one-off rider purchase does not.
mutants.first_30_days: Build a target list from public state air-permit filings for backup diesel generators, which typically list unit counts and models by phase, cross-referenced with press releases and county filings. Rank 40 campuses where permitted units far exceed operating ones. Email the procurement lead a one-page teaser: 'if your gensets shipped in Q3 2025, the OEM outer limit lands in Q1 2027'. Land three owners who hand over POs and delivery tickets for a free 5-day clock map. Use the first dated cliff to open a rider conversation with the OEM before any invoice. This also answers the parent's unresolved question of whether clocks are truly running out on unstarted equipment.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Ethyco and other Cx firms start their 10-month review after occupancy, so they sell to Cx and ops. This sells earlier, to procurement, and starts at shipment; it can also be white-labeled to them. Anyset, Nomic and Equipment Warranty Log commoditize extraction and stop at the ledger, so extraction is hidden here and the product is a dated outcome (signed deferral, accepted claim). Trane's delayed-start rider is a per-unit list product; a campus-wide negotiated deferral backed by future orders is not, and the rider becomes an input this business brokers. Wind, PV and BESS players (SGS, Sinovoltaics, TWAICE) serve other asset classes. CxPlanner and Bluerithm own punch lists, not shipment dates. Aggreko and Sunbelt Solomon are suppliers and referrers, not rivals. The judges' contingency-collection flaw is removed by leading with a fixed fee.

mutants.title: Warranty Gap Desk for MEP Contractors
mutants.one_liner: Sell to the electrical and mechanical contractors who promise owners a warranty from substantial completion while their OEM warranties run from shipment or startup, and fund the service from the contractors' own warranty reserves.
mutants.customer: The warranty manager, contracts VP or CFO at mid-size to large electrical contractors, mechanical contractors and construction managers building data centers who furnish the MEP equipment themselves (colo, enterprise and neocloud jobs, not owner-furnished hyperscale). They give the owner a 12-24 month warranty and carry a warranty reserve on the balance sheet.
mutants.problem: The parent assumed the owner feels the pain. The party actually squeezed between two clocks is the contractor. The OEM warranty passes through on an OEM calendar (startup or 18 months from ship). The contractor's promise to the owner runs from substantial completion or Tier certification, and owner-side counsel are actively advising developers to push warranty commencement to certification (the law-firm guidance in the parent's evidence). Every month of delay widens the gap, and in that gap the contractor pays for defects out of pocket. Estimators price it as a flat percentage, project managers do not track it, and closeout binders bury the OEM terms. Contractor warranty reserves are real P&L items the CFO wants released, which gives a budget line the parent never had.
mutants.solution: 1) Bid-stage gap pricing. Read the subcontract warranty clause and the OEM quotes, compute gap-days by equipment line, and price it into the bid instead of a flat reserve. 2) Deferral riders on the contractor's own POs. A contractor buying hundreds of units per year has leverage the owner lacks, and the desk pools rider purchasing across contractor clients for discounts. 3) Pre-expiry proof test and claim filing on installed gear so the OEM, not the contractor, pays for defects (load-bank partner does the physical work). 4) Reserve-release package at contract end: a documented file showing what OEM claims were accepted and what exposure remains, so the CFO can release reserve early.
mutants.why_now: Owner counsel now push warranty starts to Tier certification while long-lead delivery and phase slippage stretch the shipment-to-certification interval. Data center MEP backlogs are large, so contractors have more warranty exposure on more sites than ever. Extraction of PO, contract and OEM terms into gap-days used to require a warranty analyst per job and is now nearly free.
mutants.revenue_model: Program fee per project, roughly 0.03-0.08% of MEP contract value (about $120-320K on a $400M scope), which is a small share of a typical reserve. Assumption to validate: reserves of around 0.5-2% of contract value. Plus 20% of OEM-accepted claims that would otherwise have been borne by the contractor. Plus a rider-pooling margin or referral fee from OEMs and rental partners. Renewals follow the contractor's project pipeline, so revenue is recurring across projects.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The contractor is the only party in the chain holding an unhedged, quantifiable, budgeted warranty liability, and it is growing because of owner-side contract trends. Selling to the contractor also flips the leverage problem: one contractor buys from OEMs at volume, and a desk representing several contractors can win start-date deferrals that no single owner could. The buyer is a CFO with a reserve, not an owner's ops team with no budget.
mutants.first_30_days: Call 15 warranty managers and project executives at regional electrical and mechanical contractors with live data center work, sourced through NECA and MCAA chapters and surety brokers who track contractor exposures. Offer a free 'gap map' on two live projects using their subcontract warranty clause and OEM quotes. Target: three pilots at about $25K per project and one signed OEM rider negotiation. Confirm the key assumption early, which is what share of their data center equipment is contractor-furnished.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Ethyco and Cx firms sell warranty-phase support to owners after occupancy; the buyer here is the contractor, and the pitch is reserve release, not deficiency documentation. Anyset and Nomic sell closeout compliance to GCs and owners (is the warranty in the binder, does it match spec), while this computes the gap between the OEM clock and the contractor's obligation, buys deferrals and files OEM claims. Equipment Warranty Log and DCIM tools track expiry dates with no gap logic. Wind end-of-warranty vendors and Sinovoltaics sell to owners of other asset classes. Trane's delayed-start rider is an input purchased at pooled volume. WCS serves equipment dealers, not construction contractors, and is a possible referral partner. Aggreko and Sunbelt Solomon are load-test suppliers. Because payment comes from the contractor's reserve, the collection problem of a 25-30% contingency on 'avoided cost' owed by an owner does not arise.

mutants.title: Load-Proven Warranty Wrap for Data Halls
mutants.one_liner: Invert the parent: instead of chasing OEMs for owners as warranties expire, run a standardized load-proof test before expiry, fix what the OEM owes for free, then sell a capacity-backed warranty wrap that covers the post-expiry tail, priced from a proprietary fleet failure database.
mutants.customer: First buyers: owners and lenders' technical advisors of energized data halls approaching OEM warranty expiry, asking for a standardized Load-Proven test and certificate (a covenant-friendly document for refinancing or ABS). Later buyers: the same owners buying multi-year coverage for gensets, UPS, chillers and liquid-cooling CDUs. The capacity provider (a specialty insurer or reinsurer) is a third party in the money flow.
mutants.problem: The parent's contingency model is hard to collect and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds. Behind that is a bigger issue: once OEM warranties lapse, owners of AI halls with dense power and liquid cooling carry an unpriced failure tail, and nobody has independent load-tested failure data on these systems. OEM service contracts cover a single vendor's gear and are priced generically. Lenders financing GPU-era assets see equipment residual risk with no standard way to test or rate it.
mutants.solution: Phase 1, within 6 months: sell a standardized Load-Proven protocol. It is a 3-5 day staged load test (gensets, UPS and battery, chillers and CDUs, breakers), thermography, oil, coolant and battery diagnostics, using a load-bank rental partner and NETA-type testing subcontractors. Each test outputs a certificate and, where a defect shows, an OEM claim package while the OEM is still liable. Every test feeds a proprietary failure and degradation database. Phase 2, months 6-18: place multi-year tail coverage for tested gear through a broker or MGA partner on a quota-share basis with an insurer or reinsurer. Only gear that passed the test is bound. Defects surfaced by the test are repaired at the OEM's cost first, so the wrap covers a cleaner tail. Phase 3: become the MGA, and push the test protocol into loan covenants and insurer schedules as the standard.
mutants.why_now: AI halls introduce liquid-cooling and high-density power gear with immature public failure data, so generic pricing is either too expensive or blind. Data center lending and ABS need equipment-condition standards. Phase slippage means a large group of halls will pass through OEM expiry without ever having been stressed. Cheap LLM extraction of test logs and maintenance records lets a small team standardize reports across sites.
mutants.revenue_model: Phase 1: $60-120K per hall for the Load-Proven test (much of it load-bank pass-through), plus any claim-based fee. Phase 2: broker commission, then MGA ceding and profit commission on premium. Assumed pricing to validate with capacity providers: coverage at 1-2% of covered equipment value per year, and a 50 MW hall carries roughly $50-80M of gensets, UPS, chillers and switchgear, so about $0.5-1.6M of annual premium per hall and roughly $100-300K of commission to the MGA. That is on the order of 5-10x the parent's audit fee per hall.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The inspection is both the revenue product and the underwriting filter, and the two feed each other. Defects found pre-expiry are paid by the OEM, which reduces adverse selection, and the resulting data is a cornered resource: independent, fleet-level, load-based, across OEMs. The parent treated the warranty as an asset to recover. The bigger business treats post-warranty risk as an asset class to price, using the only thing OEMs cannot easily replicate, which is neutral cross-vendor test data.
mutants.first_30_days: Draft a two-page Load-Proven protocol with a load-bank rental partner and a NETA-type test firm. Get one data-center-finance law firm or lender's technical advisor to review a one-page covenant template. Pitch three owners with halls approaching OEM expiry and one lender with a delayed-lease loan. Meet two equipment-breakdown or specialty warranty MGAs and ask what data they would need to quote a quota-share on tested MEP gear. Goal: one paid pilot test signed and one written indication of appetite from a capacity provider.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Ethyco, Anyset, Nomic, Equipment Warranty Log and CxPlanner document, track or review; none tests under load or takes risk. Wind EOW vendors, Sinovoltaics and TWAICE are asset-class specific and stop at the claim or the analytics. OEM riders and service contracts (Trane, Cummins, Eaton) are single-vendor and priced without neutral test data, which is the wedge for an independent wrap. Aggreko and Sunbelt Solomon are hardware suppliers and channel partners. Because revenue moves from contingency-on-avoided-cost to premium, the collection and measurement flaws the judges named disappear. Defensibility comes from the failure database (cornered resource), covenant adoption (standard-setting) and later scale in premium volume.

mutants.title: Keep-the-Amps: Electrical Carve-Out for Plant Liquidations
mutants.one_liner: A 3,000-dollar electrician-verified 'in-place value memo' sold to industrial liquidators, trustees' counsel and corporate closure teams, so the switchgear and transformers are carved out of the equipment auction and sold with the real estate as a powered shell.
mutants.customer: Wedge: the 15-30 mid-size Midwest industrial liquidation auctioneers, and the panel trustees, receivers' counsel and corporate-real-estate disposition managers who hire them when a plant with at least 2 MW of service goes dark in OH, PA, MI or IN. Not manufacturers, not brokers.
mutants.problem: A plant liquidation has two teams that never talk. The equipment auctioneer sells presses, CNCs and often the switchgear, bus duct and transformers as used-equipment or scrap lots. The real-estate side lists square feet and dock doors. The energized service is the scarce asset (large transformers run about 128 weeks, switchgear 44-90+ weeks, so a buyer who has to replace them loses a year or more), and it is destroyed or stripped in the gap between the two teams. The trustee or seller has a fiduciary or financial duty to maximise proceeds but no document showing what the gear is worth in place versus removed. A secured mortgage lender and an equipment lender may also be fighting over what is a fixture.
mutants.solution: Sell one fixed-scope deliverable, the 'Powered-Shell Memo', in 8 days: (1) licensed electrician's one-day walk-through with one-line diagram, nameplates, gear age, thermography and spare capacity; (2) a carve-out schedule marking every item of electrical infrastructure as 'stays with the building' or 'safe to sell', with in-place value (replacement cost plus lead-time cost) against scrap and used-lot value; (3) utility service status (energized, disconnected, minimum-bill exposure) and a one-line check of air and wastewater permit status (shutdown, fees current, notification-only transfer), demoted to a checkbox because Ohio EPA transfer is easy; (4) a buyer-agnostic data-room cut that a data-center, battery, cold-storage or manufacturing buyer can underwrite. The fee is a flat cost line in the auction budget, paid from proceeds at closing, so the estate needs no upfront cash.
mutants.why_now: Buyers are paying for existing energized shells (TeraWulf/Anthropic's $19B lease on a shuttered aluminum plant, the former Goodyear plant in Akron running about 150 MW), and transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in years. Plant closures and manufacturer distress continue in 2026, so supply of dead plants is steady. Before the AI-power scramble a stripped switchgear lineup was worth scrap; now it is worth a year of a buyer's schedule.
mutants.revenue_model: $3,000 flat per plant (electrician cost about $1,300, analyst about 4 hours, roughly 55% gross margin), paid at closing or as a budgeted line in the liquidation. Add-ons: $1,200 buyer-ready data-room cut, $9,000 for multi-plant corporate closures (3-5 sites), and a $6k-$12k annual retainer for auctioneers who want a standing right to use the memo in their pitches. No percentage of sale price and no brokerage, which avoids the licence problem and the conflict the parent's success fee had. Later: license the anonymised gear-and-value dataset. Bottom-up: 150 to 250 qualifying Midwest industrial disposals a year at $3k-$4k is about $0.5M-$1M of report revenue for one small team before retainers, which is enough to fund the next two offspring-style expansions, not a venture-scale market by itself.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The thing that destroys the power asset in a dead plant is the equipment auction itself, not neglect. The liquidator is paid to turn gear into cash quickly, the real-estate broker never sees the gear list, and nobody owns the question 'is the switchgear worth more bolted to the building?'. The memo is not a report on the building, it is a decision document that changes what goes in the auction catalogue, and it gives the trustee defensible cover for keeping it out.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: pull 24 months of WARN closure notices for OH/PA/MI/IN, PACER Chapter 7/11 filings by manufacturers with real property, and county receivership dockets, and cross-check against Ohio EPA facility status to list about 60 dark plants with 2 MW or more. Week 2: call 15 regional liquidation auctioneers and 10 trustee counsel with one offer, a free first memo on their next live liquidation in exchange for a written case study and permission to anonymise the data. Weeks 3-4: hire one electrician for two walk-throughs at about $150 per hour; deliver memos; ask one secured mortgage lender to accept a memo as a fixture-line exhibit. Success test: at least one auctioneer pulls electrical gear from a catalogue, and two of the next three mandates pay $3,000 at closing.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: It is not a listing or parcel-scoring database, so it steps around Brownfield.ai, Scout, ZoomProspector, LandGate and Enverus, which all sell search or grid-level screening to buyers. The payer is the seller side at the moment of disposition, which none of them serve, and JobsOhio, AEP and FirstEnergy databases are free but verify sites and service, not gear or carve-out decisions. PCA and electrical inspection firms give buyers a compliance-style ampacity line; nobody gives a seller a valued in-place versus scrap schedule tied to the auction terms. The permit-transferability wedge that was thin in the parent is reduced to a checkbox, and the success fee is dropped.

mutants.title: Load Recovery for Municipal Utilities and Co-ops
mutants.one_liner: Sell the verified dead-plant record to the municipal electric utilities and rural co-ops that lose money every month the anchor plant sits dark, priced as a package plus a bonus tied to the load they get back.
mutants.customer: Municipal electric systems, rural electric co-ops and their joint-action agencies or statewide associations (for example American Municipal Power and the state municipal electric associations) in OH, PA, MI and IN, where an anchor industrial plant has closed and the utility's own economic-development or general manager decides. Wedge: 8 utilities in the Mahoning Valley, Akron/Canton and western PA with an idle plant of at least 2 MW in their territory.
mutants.problem: When a plant with several MW of load closes, a small public utility keeps paying its fixed wholesale power, transmission and substation costs but spreads them over fewer kWh, so rates rise for homes and shops and the remaining industrial customers get nervous (an assumption to validate with 10 utility managers). These utilities have no economic-development staff, are ignored by the investor-owned-utility databases and grid-analytics vendors, and cannot tell a data-center or battery developer what is actually inside the fence of their dead plant. Meanwhile the plant's energized service, which the utility itself installed and meters, is the one asset that could replace the lost load.
mutants.solution: A 'Load Recovery Package' per idle plant: (1) electrician-verified one-line diagram, gear nameplates, spare capacity and slab/crane condition; (2) the utility's own historical interval load and substation loading, which only the utility holds, turned into a stranded-load scorecard showing what re-energizing 2, 4 or 8 MW would do to fixed-cost recovery and rates; (3) a pre-cleared economic-development rate rider and a written will-serve position, drafted with the utility's engineer, which is the hardest input in the parent's product and is free when the utility is the customer; (4) outreach to a curated buyer list (manufacturers, battery and cold-storage operators, small data-center and inference developers) with the record as the data room. Later, a member-services version sold through a joint-action agency to all members.
mutants.why_now: Buyers with real money now want existing energized industrial shells, so a dead plant in a small utility's territory has more than one class of possible buyer for the first time in decades. Large-load tariffs and interconnection queues at the big investor-owned utilities push developers to look for capacity elsewhere, and roughly 128-week transformer lead times make existing service worth years. Ohio's 125+ local data-center moratoriums are a problem for pure data-center strategies, so a buyer-agnostic pitch to friendly municipal utilities is safer.
mutants.revenue_model: $9,500 per Load Recovery Package paid from the utility's economic-development budget; $18,000 per year retainer covering up to five sites, buyer outreach and a rolling record refresh; a capped performance bonus of about 10% of the first-year demand-charge margin from re-energized load (cap around $60k), structured as an economic-development services fee from the utility and not a commission on a property sale (have Ohio counsel confirm the real-estate licence question before signing). Channel: a joint-action agency or state association licenses the tool to members at $40k-$80k per year. Bottom-up: about 100-150 qualifying utilities in four states at an average $12k in year one is $1.2M-$1.8M, with 70-plus percent gross margin after the electrician cost on the package.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The utility, not the broker or the manufacturer, is the party that already holds the two hardest inputs, years of interval meter data on the dead plant and the ability to say in writing what it would take to re-energize it, and it is also the only party that loses money every month the plant stays dark. Sell to them and the will-serve letter that costs the parent weeks of chasing becomes something the customer hands you. Small public utilities are also unserved by every funded competitor, which all chase hyperscalers and the big investor-owned utilities.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: build a list of every municipal electric system and co-op in northeast Ohio and western PA (from state association member lists) and match each to idle plants using Ohio EPA and county parcel data; shortlist 20 with a dark plant of at least 2 MW. Weeks 2-3: call 20 general managers and superintendents; pitch a free 'stranded-load scorecard' on their dead plant using their meter data. Get three to share interval data and access. Week 4: deliver one scorecard plus a paid quote of $9,500 for the full package, and pitch a 20-minute slot at a state municipal electric association meeting. Success test: one utility signs the $9,500 package or a letter of intent, and one association agrees to a member pilot.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: GridCARE, LandGate, Enverus and Paces work at substation and grid level for data-center developers and large investor-owned utilities, and none inspect inside the fence. AEP, FirstEnergy, JobsOhio and ZoomProspector are free or embedded databases of sites and buildings that do not verify gear and are irrelevant to small public utilities without such programs. Scout and Brownfield.ai are network and listing platforms for buyers and owners with no utility-side product and no meter data. The customer here has no productised alternative, only the general manager's phone calls, and the utility's own data is a cornered resource the funded competitors cannot get at a small utility unless they are invited in.

mutants.title: Keep-Warm: Preserving Power in Idle Plants
mutants.one_liner: Invert the database: instead of scoring dead plants once, sell a monthly service that keeps their electrical service alive and monitored, then turn 200 preserved shells into a right-of-first-offer inventory and, later, a balance-sheet powered-shell bank.
mutants.customer: Wedge: banks, special servicers and lenders holding real-estate-owned industrial plants, plus corporate owners of mothballed plants and county land banks, in the Mahoning Valley and Akron/Canton first. Later buyers: data-center, battery and manufacturing developers who pay for shells certified 'energized-ready'.
mutants.problem: An idle plant's electrical system is a wasting asset on a clock. Standard commercial property policies limit cover for vandalism, theft, water damage and sprinkler leakage once a building has been vacant for about 60 days (an assumption to verify with an insurance broker), copper theft and roof leaks wreck switchgear, utilities can pull service or reclassify accounts on idle meters, oil-filled transformers degrade, and permit fees and reports lapse. Residential-style property-preservation firms winterize and change locks, but nobody is paid to preserve amps. Owners find out the plant is worth far less than it was only when a buyer's electrician opens the gear two years later.
mutants.solution: Two tiers. 'Watch' at $650 per month: baseline electrician record (the Power Passport becomes the set-up fee), a $600 sensor kit (humidity, temperature, door, current clamps on the main service, cellular camera), quarterly thermography, and an insurer-facing monthly report. 'Warm' at $2,200 per month: monthly electrician visits, keep-energized management with the utility including minimum-bill and account status, annual transformer oil sampling, dehumidification, theft-alarm response and permit fee and report compliance. The continuous data produces an 'energized-ready' score, days to first power, and a verified time series no one-off inspection can match. Marketing and right-of-first-offer rights are bundled into the contract for owners who want a sale.
mutants.why_now: Low-cost cellular sensors and cameras collapsed to tens of dollars a unit. Vision models now read nameplates and gear photos cheaply, which cuts analyst hours per building. More industrial shells are going idle while buyers now pay a premium for existing power, so, for the first time, preserving the electrical system has a positive return.
mutants.revenue_model: Recurring: $650 or $2,200 per building per month plus a $2,500 baseline record; a carry-cost comparison shows a 300k sq ft idle plant costing an owner roughly $15k-$40k per month, so the service is 3-8% on top of existing carry. Gross margin about 50-55% at 10 buildings per electrician route. Insurer angle: partner with a vacant-property insurance managing general agent to turn monitoring into a rating credit, which can pay for itself. Scale path: 200 buildings on Warm and Watch is about $4M-$5M annual recurring revenue; the contract's right of first offer gives inventory to sell to buyers on a fee basis; a later fund of $50M-$100M exercises options on the best 20 shells, subdivides them into permitted 'factory condos' or powered shells and sells or leases at a premium. First 6 months: 5-8 paying buildings.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The same service that stops the asset dying also builds the only dataset that matters: a time series of load, temperature, humidity and access on hundreds of idle industrial buildings, and exclusive access to a pipeline of them. That combination is a cornered resource plus a switching cost, defended by contracts and data history and not by scoring algorithms anyone can copy. The parent is a snapshot; this is the movie, and a monthly bill is a better business than a report.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: list 40 idle plants owned by banks, special servicers and land banks from county auditor and REO data in two metros; contact 8 REO and asset managers. Week 2: call two vacant-property insurance brokers and one managing general agent to test whether monitoring earns a premium credit or a vacancy-clause endorsement (the riskiest assumption). Weeks 3-4: sign three 90-day pilots on Watch at a waived set-up fee in exchange for a case study and marketing rights, install kits, and deliver the first insurer-facing report. Success test: one lender converts to $650 per month paid and one insurer or broker confirms a written premium credit or vacancy accommodation.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: None of the parent's competitors monitor or preserve anything. Brownfield.ai, Scout, LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces and ZoomProspector sell data or listings, and JobsOhio and the utility databases are free lists. PCA and electrical inspection firms sell a one-time report, and residential property-preservation and big facilities-management firms cover occupied, high-value assets or locks and lawns, not energized-capacity preservation. The business is recurring service revenue with a proprietary time series, so a funded data competitor would have to hire electricians and sign owner contracts to copy it, and the exclusive marketing rights become a cornered resource.

mutants.title: Pooled Calendar Reporters for Limited-Scope Family Lawyers
mutants.one_liner: One physically present reporter sits an entire family-court calendar and sells the record by the matter, about $110 per 15-minute hearing, so each lawyer pays roughly 75% less than a half-day pro tem while the reporter earns more than a normal pro tem day.
mutants.customer: Wedge: limited-scope (unbundled) and solo family-law attorneys who appear on DVRO, custody and support calendars in ONE high-volume California courthouse, plus the non-indigent 'missing middle' litigants they represent, who fail the fee-waiver test but cannot spend $450 on a record. Not indigent litigants (the FVAP ruling moves them to a court-paid record) and not the court.
mutants.problem: About 7 in 10 civil, family and probate hearings in California have no verbatim record, and appeals of custody and restraining-order rulings fail without one. Courts tell litigants to 'arrange your own' reporter, but a private pro tem costs $450-500 for a half day, and no one pays that for a 12-minute item. The parent's fix (remote reporters dialing in) is barred by Gov. Code 69959 and by the 69959.5 pilot limits, so it cannot launch as written. The parent also has no proof that anyone will pay $95, and the ruling shrinks the legal-aid segment.
mutants.solution: Drop remote reporting and prediction. A reporter is physically in the department for the whole morning or afternoon calendar, which is the lawful 'bring your own reporter' route. Attorneys book a matter slot the day before at $110 for up to 15 minutes, plus a per-page certified transcript (about $8/page) only if they order one. Booking is all-or-nothing, like a crowdfund: the reporter goes only if at least 6-8 matters are booked by 5pm the day before, otherwise everyone is refunded. That kills the dead-time problem without any duration model. Each party gets only its own matter's transcript, and other matters on the reporter's notes are never released. Cross-department hopping and duration prediction come later, once the manual logs give real data. Unit economics (assumptions to test): 2 sessions/day x 8 matters x $110 = $1,760 gross. The reporter keeps about 60% ($1,056) versus $900-1,000 for two half-day pro tem bookings, and the company keeps about $700 per reporter-day before ops.
mutants.why_now: FVAP v. Superior Court (Aug 10, 2026) put the 70% no-record gap in every family lawyer's inbox. It also makes courts serve only indigent litigants, which leaves a large paying middle. Courts are already telling family litigants in writing to arrange their own reporter. The reporter shortage (about 5,500 short by 2030) means freelancers can choose better-paying days, so a higher-yield day is a real recruiting pitch.
mutants.revenue_model: $110 per matter slot for up to 15 minutes, $8/page for certified transcripts, and prepaid 5-packs ($500) for cash up front. The reporter keeps about 60% of slot fees, the platform keeps about 40% (about 35% gross margin after the payment and ops costs of a services business). Year-2 add-ons: a subscription for attorneys who book 8+ hearings a month, and referral-funded 'record scholarships' from DV appellate nonprofits.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Once the first attorney in a department triggers the reporter's presence, every other matter that day costs roughly nothing extra, so the price can fall 75% while the reporter's day pay rises. Limited-scope attorneys are the right buyer because they bill flat per hearing and can pass the record fee through as an itemized line, while a full-service litigator does not think of the record as a per-hearing line item. The tipping-point booking rule replaces the prediction model the parent needed.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: one-week legal check with a court-reporter licensing attorney and the clerks of the 2 target departments (private pro tem in the room, multiple parties sharing one reporter, closed-hearing rules, and any court-reporting-firm registration). Weeks 1-2: pick the single biggest family courthouse in one county, recruit 3 physically local pro tem reporters, and pre-sell 5-packs to 15 limited-scope attorneys from the family-law bar and unbundled-services listservs. Weeks 3-4: run the first 10 calendars with a Google Sheet, Stripe links and a group text, using the booking threshold, and log booked-matter density and actual call order per department. Offer FVAP and one DV appellate nonprofit free slots for cases they flag as appeal-bound.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Steno, DirectDep, StenoScout and the agencies (Veritext, Esquire and others) sell a whole appearance to one buyer, mostly depositions, so every buyer pays the full minimum, and their half-day minimum is structural. We sell the matter, split one appearance across many paying parties, and stay lawful without remote reporting. The AB 3013 pilot covers only court-employed reporters in a court facility, capped at 10-20% of reporters in 13 counties. We serve paying litigants in any county and do not compete for the court-employed slots. eScribers and Verbit transcribe recordings, which fits the court's indigent fallback but not an attorney who wants a stenographic record, live and immediate. The moat, if the wedge works, is proprietary calendar density and call-order data per department, and reporter loyalty from the higher day yield, which points to a cornered-resource advantage in one courthouse before any scale.

mutants.title: Record-on-Request Desk for Superior Courts
mutants.one_liner: A managed compliance service that lets a superior court answer any indigent litigant's request for a verbatim record with one certified record per request, priced per record delivered and using the cheapest lawful method, whether steno or electronic recording.
mutants.customer: Court executive officers and presiding family/probate judges of small and mid-size California superior courts, especially those outside the AB 3013 pilot or above its 10-20% cap. Self-represented litigants and DV legal aid are the users, but the court is the payer.
mutants.problem: FVAP v. Superior Court (Aug 10, 2026) gives indigent litigants a mandatory right to an official verbatim record on request, through court-paid pro tem reporters or electronic recording. Courts have no reporters and hiring freezes, and they cannot staff for requests that could arrive any day. Their real gap is a defensible request-to-record workflow: intake, indigency check, method selection, delivery of a certified appeal-ready record, and reporting. The 3 million hearings without a record are already a Judicial Council-visible metric. Half-day pro tem minimums make each request cost $450-500 or more.
mutants.solution: A per-request desk, priced by outcome. The litigant or facilitator files a request when they set the hearing, so the desk usually gets 2-7 days of notice, which turns random demand into schedulable demand. The desk picks the method: (a) the court's own recording plus a certified transcript on demand (subcontracted to an eScribers-style vendor), or (b) a physically present steno reporter from a pooled roster that covers several requests in the same courthouse (the offspring-1 network) when a steno record is required or the department has no recording. The court pays only for records delivered and certified. A dashboard shows requests, turnaround and no-record rate by department, ready for Judicial Council reporting. The desk is offered at no retainer with a quarterly spend cap, sized to the court's own budget.
mutants.why_now: The Supreme Court decision is Aug 2026 and the court decision names the compliance routes, so every court now needs a plan, and no incumbent has packaged one. Reporter budgets and vacancy savings exist because courts cannot fill positions, and CA has already sent dedicated funding to court reporters (verify the current allocation and whether vacancy savings can be redirected). Verbit's Judicial Council master agreement for captioning from July 1, 2026 shows courts do buy court-tech through master agreements, which gives a path from single-court pilots to statewide.
mutants.revenue_model: The court pays a flat $150-250 per hearing record delivered (up to 30 minutes), certified transcripts at a per-page rate, and no retainer. Pricing sits below a $450-500 half-day pro tem and far below an idle full-time reporter. Steno requests use pooled reporters, and audio requests use subcontracted transcription, so gross margin is about 30-40%. Year 2: annual subscription for the dashboard and intake software, and a statewide master-agreement bid. Legal aid and foundations can fund 'request navigators' who file requests for litigants, which lifts volume.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The court does not need reporters. It needs a defensible answer to a request, so the method is irrelevant, and the biggest threat (electronic recording) becomes a supply input to a desk that will choose it. Requests that arrive at intake instead of at the courtroom door are what make pooled steno economical, because notice converts unpredictable demand into a schedule. Outcome pricing ('pay only when a certified record is delivered') is the contingency that lets a risk-averse court say yes without a retainer.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: one-week legal check with a court-reporter licensing attorney, plus reading the ruling's list of lawful compliance routes. Weeks 1-3: ask FVAP and 2-3 DV legal-aid groups to introduce court executives of two counties with the highest no-record rates. Build the intake form and an eScribers-style subcontract, and sign 3 physical pro tem reporters in one county. Weeks 3-4: offer one family department a no-cost, at-cost 60-day compliance pilot (about 20-40 requests) with a weekly report. Aim for an under-threshold purchase order or sole-source urgent-compliance pilot within 90-120 days. The 30-day success test is a signed pilot letter from one court and a design-partner agreement with FVAP.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Steno, DirectDep and StenoScout sell to attorneys, mostly depositions, and have no intake, indigency, certification or reporting workflow for courts. The incumbent agencies sell courts half-day pro tem bookings, which is the price the desk undercuts. eScribers and Verbit transcribe recordings but do not handle request intake, method choice or physical steno backup, so they are supply partners, not rivals. The AB 3013 pilot is court-employed, capped and in 13 counties; we serve every court above the cap or outside the pilot. The main threat is a court building intake in-house or a Judicial Council master agreement commoditizing the service, so the plan is to be on the master agreement's vendor list early and to own the request-intake data.

mutants.title: Courtroom ETA: Call-Time Network for Family Court
mutants.one_liner: A 'FlightAware for family court calendars' that texts litigants, lawyers and freelance reporters and interpreters their predicted call time, giving the queue away and selling the same feed to the professionals who lose half-day minimums waiting.
mutants.customer: Start: DV survivors and family litigants (free, via legal-aid and DV org sponsors) and solo family-law attorneys ($29/month). Paying side by month 6: freelance court reporters, interpreters and appearance attorneys who buy call-time alerts to hop between hearings. Later: courts, which pay for staggered 'time-certain' calendars.
mutants.problem: Family calendars run on the 8:30 cattle call: 30-40 matters set at one time and called in an order nobody can see. Parties, including survivors who may wait near their abuser, sit in a hallway for hours. Attorneys burn billable time (a solo lawyer's 2-hour wait costs $400-600, an assumption to verify). Reporters, interpreters and appearance counsel price by the half day because no one can predict a 15-minute call time. The parent's dispatch model needed that prediction but assumed it was a feature, when it is the missing infrastructure for every short-hearing service.
mutants.solution: Inverted product: prediction first, services second. Month 1-6 product: an SMS bot for two departments in one courthouse. A litigant or attorney texts a case number and gets 'about 45 minutes; you are 9th of 34'. Data comes from the public daily calendar, historical durations by hearing type and judge, and check-ins: people text 'called' or 'out' from the hallway (not from inside the courtroom, where phones may be restricted), plus paid spotters logging call order at $18/hour for the first 20 court days. Publish a per-department 'wait report card' as press and leverage. The same feed then powers a services layer, with reporters, interpreters and appearance attorneys buying alerts and booking one hearing at a time, which turns the parent's marketplace into the second product. Endgame: the call-time index becomes the standard that courts license to stagger calendars.
mutants.why_now: After the FVAP decision the gap in recorded hearings is public news. Courts, legal aid and press now treat family-court process failures as a story. Cheap SMS, LLM-based calendar parsing and speech-to-text make the data layer nearly free, while calendar data has been public but unused for years. The reporter shortage forces reporters to hop to survive, and the shortage gives them an incentive to pay for the ETA.
mutants.revenue_model: Free for litigants (sponsored by DV legal aid, foundation and IOLTA-type grants). $29/month for attorneys. $99-299/month per reporter, interpreter or appearance attorney for alerts and hop scheduling, plus a booking fee (10-15%) once the per-hearing marketplace exists. Courts pay for calendar analytics and a staggering tool ($20-60K per court per year, an assumption) after the wait report cards create pressure. Bottom-up illustration to test: 40 family departments x 30 matters x 2 parties is about 2,400 party-attendances/day in one large county.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The reporting shortage is a symptom of an information problem: half-day minimums exist because the call time is unknowable. Give the information away to the crowd and charge the people who can turn it into utilization. Each check-in improves the ETA for everyone else in the department (network effect), so density in a courthouse is the moat, and the data is a cornered resource no reporter agency can copy without the crowd. It also fixes the parent's legal flaw: it needs no remote reporting, only public calendars and voluntary check-ins.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: choose the two busiest family departments in one large county, hire two spotters (retired court watchers or paralegal students) and log call order and durations for 20 court days. Week 2: build a Twilio SMS bot with a manual ETA rule (calendar position x median duration by hearing type). Week 3: recruit 10 solo attorneys and 2 DV legal-aid groups as first users, and 3 freelance interpreters or reporters as paying alerts customers. Week 4: publish the first department wait report card and test whether hallway wait shrinks and whether any reporter will pay $99/month. Day 180 target: 300 active attorneys and litigants in one courthouse, 20 paying professionals, and a second courthouse.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: None of the parent's competitors predicts call time. Steno, DirectDep and StenoScout are booking marketplaces for depositions and would be buyers of the feed, not rivals. Incumbent agencies sell half-day pro tem, which is what the ETA erodes. eScribers and Verbit handle records after the fact, and the AB 3013 pilot is court-employed reporting. The one adjacent category I could not check (search budget exhausted) is court-date reminder apps, which remind people of the date but, as far as I know, do not rank queue position within a calendar. Verify that before building. Main risks: courts restricting phone use or check-ins, and calendar data quality, so the first release relies on spotters and public calendars.

mutants.title: Camp-Road Closing Rescue Plus Resale Toll
mutants.one_liner: A Maine-only, attorney-supervised service that runs the statutory neighbor meeting, records an enforceable assessment-lien covenant, and then issues a paid road-status letter on every future sale on that road.
mutants.customer: Wedge: closing attorneys and title agents handling lake-camp, second-home and rural sales in Maine's lakes region and midcoast (start with the 5 to 8 firms that do the most camp closings). The payer at the table is the seller, or the buyer via negotiated credit. Out-of-state second-home buyers and their lenders are the ones who insist on a maintenance agreement. Listing agents are a secondary channel in the Oct-Feb off-season, when they prep camps for spring listing.
mutants.problem: Maine Title 23 section 3101 (text re-checked today) lets as few as 3 parcels petition a notary to call a meeting, lets a majority vote set assessments, and shields board members from civil liability. It contains no lien or collection remedy. The parent research counted 4 parcels, but the fetched text says 3 parcels held by 3 different owners. So the statute is a vote without teeth, and nobody runs the vote. No closing attorney will chase 14 owners for proxies at a flat closing fee, so the sale stalls or closes on a handshake. The parent's own flaws sit on top of this. Its $12-25 per household per month is 6 to 12 times PayHOA's price anchor. Holding dues float triggers trust-account rules. A 5-8% procurement fee is a conflict of interest. Its plan to have attorneys send deals for a flat fee is a RESPA Section 8 trap, because 12 CFR 1024.14 bars referral fees and unearned fees in federally related mortgage transactions and permits payment only for services actually performed.
mutants.solution: Sell 'Meeting-in-a-Box' as a fixed-scope, attorney-supervised package. We do the non-billable grunt work: map benefiting parcels from the registry of deeds and county GIS, serve statutory notice, run the notary-called meeting (in person plus absentee and proxy ballots), keep minutes, collect the officer slate and a treasurer, take a baseline road-condition photo log, and handle recording. The supervising attorney, either the closing attorney or our contracted Maine counsel, owns the legal instrument: a recorded covenant that adds what the statute lacks (assessment lien running with the land, successor obligation, reserve requirement, estoppel-letter mechanism). We build no dues software and hold no money. Each association opens a bank account with a treasurer, and we hand over a checklist plus a PayHOA or plain-ACH setup guide. After formation we run one annual notice-and-meeting cycle and issue a road-status letter (dues current, no open assessments, maintenance agreement on record) whenever a house on the road sells. This works like the HOA resale certificate. No referral fees are paid to anyone. Attorneys bill their own legal work, and our fee is a disclosed third-party service line.
mutants.why_now: Maine's statute already exists, so formation is process work rather than a legal breakthrough. Post-2020 in-migration put many out-of-state buyers on camp roads they do not understand. Housing turnover is historically low (roughly 3-4% a year, an assumption to confirm), so every stalled closing costs a seller and an agent real money. Hurricane Helene's NC private-road program showed that aid and repair money flow only to an organized counterparty with a named contact, which makes 'pre-formed association' a sellable feature. Oct-Feb is slack season for Maine camp closings, so attorneys have time to try a new workflow before spring listings. Cheap document automation and e-signature make proxy and absentee ballot logistics a small cost rather than a paralegal week.
mutants.revenue_model: Formation: $1,400 flat per road, paid at closing from seller proceeds or by the neighborhood, disclosed as a third-party service. Attorney legal review is billed separately by the attorney at roughly $300-500. Recurring: $200 per association per year, flat rather than per household, for annual notice, meeting, officer changes and records. Transaction toll: $175 per road-status letter, paid by the seller at each future sale. With about 9 coordinator hours plus recording fees per formation, gross margin should be near 60-65%. Rough year-1 target is 40 roads, or about $56k formation plus $8k recurring. At 300 roads with about 18 homes each and 3-4% turnover, resale letters add about $35k a year. That makes a real but modest Maine business, and the scalable asset is the state-by-state playbook plus the registry.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing in Maine is not the entity, since the statute lets neighbors make one, and not the legal template, which is a commodity. It is the person who runs the meeting and the recorded covenant that gives assessments teeth. The first closing buys the association, and every later closing pays a toll, so a formed road becomes a perpetual, transaction-priced revenue stream. That toll avoids the PayHOA per-household price anchor and sits where the money is, in seller proceeds. Because the attorney does the legal work under supervision and is never paid to refer, the attorney channel is RESPA-clean and the attorney stops being the substitute. Over time title agents learn to ask for our letter, which creates switching costs because the association's officer and records live with us.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: retain a Maine real estate attorney on a flat $3-5k engagement to draft the covenant with lien language, the estoppel-letter form and the meeting script. Have that attorney confirm the lien is enforceable when drafted as a recorded covenant and confirm the RESPA-safe fee structure. Weeks 1-3: hold 20 calls with lakes-region and midcoast closing attorneys and title agents and ask which of their last 12 months' closings hit a road issue, what happened, and what they would pay to have it handled. Weeks 2-4: run 2 pilot roads (one tied to a live or stalled closing) at a $600 pilot price, and measure owner participation rate, days to majority vote, and hours per road. By day 30, get 3 firms to sign a one-page agreement to route their next road problem to us at $1,400. The riskiest assumption to kill early is whether attorneys will buy outsourced meeting logistics rather than absorb it.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: PayHOA: we build no dues product and do not compete at about $2 per household. We price per association and per sale, and PayHOA is a setup option we recommend, so it is a partner rather than a rival. Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC: they serve incorporated associations with managers, whereas we create the legal counterparty they cannot. DIY templates and local attorneys (Nolo, LegalZoom-style forms): a template gives no notice, vote, proxy, minutes or recording service, and the attorney is our channel and supervising counsel rather than a substitute, because we take the work they cannot bill profitably. Maine statute: we productize it and plug its missing lien with the recorded covenant. NC Private Road and Bridge Program: a demand signal, and our 'pre-formed association with a named contact' is exactly what such programs require. Local road-association managers and bookkeepers (unidentified): they sell ongoing bookkeeping, not closing-triggered formation, and could be subcontractors for annual administration.

mutants.title: Town-Paid Private Road Census and Formation Bounty
mutants.one_liner: Sell New England towns (and their municipal insurance pools) a four-week census of every private road's legal status and emergency-access risk, then earn a per-road bounty for each neighbor group converted into a recorded association with a named point of contact.
mutants.customer: Town managers, road commissioners and fire chiefs of small and mid-sized Maine towns (2,000-15,000 residents), then NH and VT. Multi-town buyers: regional councils and planning commissions, and municipal risk pools that fund loss-control services for member towns (Maine Municipal Association's risk program, NH Primex, Vermont VLCT PACIF, all from prior knowledge and unverified here). Secondary payers: developers, via a road-association setup line on the town's subdivision application fee. Residents co-pay a small share.
mutants.problem: Every town has dozens to hundreds of private ways with unknown legal status. The town usually cannot spend public money on them (varies by state, to be confirmed per state), yet it is blamed when an ambulance or plow cannot pass a failed culvert, when a subdivision road approved on the condition that a road association be formed decays years later, or when residents petition the town to accept a broken road that would cost six figures to rebuild to town standard. After a storm, state aid wants an organized counterparty. NC's post-Helene private-road program (verified) required a single point of contact and proof of ownership, plus a 50% cost share. The town has no inventory to hand over. Neighbors are stuck in a collective-action deadlock, because nobody wants to be the one who calls the meeting.
mutants.solution: Step 1, a fixed-price Private Road Census, roughly $6,500 per town. We ingest parcel GIS, E911 road-name files, registry-of-deeds documents and any culvert or bridge inventory the town has. Language models read the recorded instruments to flag whether a maintenance agreement exists and what it says. For each private way we output parcels served, recorded instrument yes/no, whether an active association exists, contact if any, single-access and stream-crossing flags, and a fire-truck-passability risk score reviewed with the fire chief. The town gets a ranked list, map and memo. Step 2, activation. The town mails a letter on its own letterhead to the top 40 roads with a pre-filled petition for the statutory meeting. In Maine a few owners can petition a notary, and the town letter breaks the who-goes-first deadlock. We run the meetings, and an attorney-supervised covenant is recorded. The town pays a $600 bounty for each completed association (recorded instrument plus officers and point of contact), and residents co-pay about $500. Step 3, a registry subscription at about $2,400 per town per year. It keeps contacts, insurance certificates, reserve attestations and condition photos current, and yields a disaster-ready roads list for the state emergency agency after a storm. Step 4, the town adds a setup fee to subdivision applications so new roads get an association and reserve schedule at approval.
mutants.why_now: The cost stack collapsed. Reading recorded instruments for 120 roads used to mean about 120 title searches at hundreds of dollars each. With document extraction plus human QA it is roughly a tenth of that, which is what makes a fixed-price census possible. Storm events keep exposing the same gap, and NC's $175M program (verified) shows states will pay for repair but only through an organized counterparty. Parcel GIS and E911 layers are now open in most New England states. Municipal risk pools are always looking for loss-control programs to justify member subsidies (hypothesis to test). The disaster-aid windows (NC applications closed Feb 2026) show that the next program will again favor roads that are already organized.
mutants.revenue_model: Census $6,500 per town, or a regional-council package of 10-12 towns at about $55-65k. Formation bounty $600 per association from the town, plus a $500 resident co-pay, or about $1,100 per road. Registry $2,400 per town per year. Developer setup fee about $1,200 per new subdivision, collected through the town. A town with 120 private ways where 60% are informal has about 70 candidates. If 40% convert in year 1, that is 28 roads, about $31k in bounties and co-pays, plus census and registry, or about $40k per town in year 1. 25 towns would be about $1M. Conversion rate is the key hypothesis. Risk pools could subsidize the census for members, making the insurer a second payer.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The town is not buying road repairs or software. It is buying a legal counterparty for roads it cannot touch, plus a defensible record that it knew about the risk and acted. That is liability hygiene, an easier budget line than subsidizing private roads. The official letter is the cheapest neighbor-activation channel that exists, because it dissolves the who-goes-first deadlock that makes formation so slow closing-by-closing. One buyer delivers dozens of roads, which inverts the parent's per-road CAC. The census data, once assembled across towns, becomes a state-level inventory that emergency agencies, lenders and title underwriters would pay for.
mutants.first_30_days: Pick one pilot town with open parcel GIS and online registry access, ideally a lakes-region Maine town of about 4,000 people. Build a free 30-road slice of the census in 10 days from public data. Walk it to the road commissioner, fire chief and town manager, and ask them for the 5 roads they fear most. Ask to mail an official letter to 10 pilot roads and run 2 statutory meetings within 30 days. In parallel, call 3 regional councils and the risk-management teams of the Maine, NH and Vermont municipal associations to test whether they would subsidize census work as loss control. Target one signed $4,500 first-town census (typically under small-purchase thresholds, to be confirmed) and one pilot association recorded. Riskiest assumptions: town willingness to pay a per-road bounty, and letter-to-meeting conversion above 25%.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: PayHOA and the mainstream HOA platforms: they sell to associations and managers, never to towns, and require an existing association. We create the association, and dues admin stays a thin link to whatever tool the road picks. DIY templates and local attorneys: they serve a single closing, and we are town-sponsored and mass-produced with attorney supervision behind it, so we are a customer of their legal review rather than a rival. State statutes and county road districts: we operationalize the statute at scale for towns rather than asking residents to self-serve. NC Private Road and Bridge Program: a demand proof and a template for who will need our pre-qualified registry after the next storm. Local road-association managers (unidentified): potential subcontractors for annual administration, not competitors for a town-level census. Town asset-management and GIS vendors such as Cartegraph or OpenGov (from prior knowledge, unverified): they track public roads and would not create legal counterparties on private ones.

mutants.title: Contractor-First Road Billing, Then Repair Lending
mutants.one_liner: Invert the parent: sell to plow and gravel contractors who each serve dozens of handshake roads with a get-paid rail that binds every household to its share, then use the payment history and recorded covenants to become the lender for culvert and washout repairs no bank will touch.
mutants.customer: Wedge: independent plow, gravel and excavation contractors serving 15-80 private roads and shared driveways each, starting in one snow-belt county in Maine or NH. Later payers: road associations as borrowers, and community banks, credit unions and CDFIs as capital partners who buy participations in the loans we originate and service.
mutants.problem: A contractor plows a 12-home road on a verbal 'we'll split it'. He bills one neighbor, who fronts the money and chases the others. After one or two free-riders the fronting neighbor quits, so the contractor drops the road or absorbs the loss. Contractors also front fuel, labor and equipment for a season and are paid unevenly. When a culvert or bridge fails, a $30-150k repair has no borrower, since there is no entity, no assets and no financials. NC's post-Helene program (verified) demanded a 50% cost share, a single point of contact and proof of ownership, so roads that could not front cash and had no organization were shut out. Both sides of the road are cash-starved for the same reason, which is no legal counterparty.
mutants.solution: Phase 1, sold this October to be live by first snow. RoadPay for contractors: the contractor enters a road's seasonal price. Each household receives an e-sign Road Service Agreement (pro-rata formula, driveway-level opt-in, dispute rule) with autopay via Stripe Connect direct charges, so we never hold funds. The contractor gets one dashboard across all roads, automatic reminders and statements, and monthly payouts. Phase 2, winter: Season Advance. We advance 60-80% of a signed road's seasonal contract to the contractor, funded by a small credit line, and repay ourselves from the households' autopay through April. We underwrite at the road level using percent of households on autopay, contractor history and driveway geometry. Phase 3, year 2: Graduation. Roads with two clean seasons are invited to record an assessment-lien covenant (through the closing-rescue-style formation service), because it lowers their borrowing rate. Phase 4: Repair and cost-share bridge loans. $25-150k loans to the association for culverts, regrading and bridge repairs, repaid over 5-10 years from assessments, funded by CDFI and community-bank participation with us as originator and servicer. The same facility can bridge the up-front 50% of state reimbursement programs.
mutants.why_now: Winter 2026-27 seasonal contracts get signed in October and November, about six weeks from today. That gives a hard deadline and a full season of data inside a six-month window. Embedded payments are now a commodity (Stripe Connect handles onboarding, split payouts and money-movement compliance), which is the Wardley shift that makes a two-person team viable. Post-Helene aid design (verified) teaches that organized counterparties get capital and unorganized roads do not. Document extraction makes reading recorded covenants cheap enough to underwrite each road. Contractor cost inflation since 2021 plausibly makes non-payment more painful (hypothesis to test in interviews).
mutants.revenue_model: Phase 1: 4% of billings collected, paid by the contractor (no per-household fee, so the PayHOA $2 anchor never applies). Phase 2: 3-5% fee on advances, turned several times per season. Phase 4: 2-3% origination plus about 1.5% servicing on loans sold to bank partners, plus net interest on any retained slice. Illustration: 100 contractors x 40 roads x $3,000 is about $12M of billings, so about $480k of rail revenue. If 5% of roads borrow $60k a year, that is about $12M of loans and roughly $300-500k of origination and servicing. Early revenue is small. The business becomes large only if the payment history and lien-backed collateral become the standard underwriting file for private roads, which is the 10x claim.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The party with the best data and the strongest incentive is the contractor, not the neighbors. He knows every road's parcels, who pays, and which culvert is about to fail, and one phone call reaches 40 roads. His invoice is a high-frequency touchpoint neighbors already accept, whereas a formation package is a rare, compliance-flavored purchase. The legal entity stops being a product and becomes collateral. Neighbors will sign a recorded covenant to cut their repair loan rate from, say, 14% to 8%, which they would never do for 'compliance'. It also removes the parent's conflict of interest, since the contractor is the customer rather than a party we take a procurement fee from.
mutants.first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 plow and gravel contractors in one county through local snow-removal and excavation groups, feed and hardware stores and Facebook groups, and offer free first-season setup on their 3 most annoying roads. Have an attorney spend $2-4k reviewing a generic Road Service Agreement and consumer-ACH disclosures. Build a no-code MVP in 2 weeks (contractor form, e-sign page, Stripe Connect autopay, manual reconciliation sheet). Convert at least 25 roads before first snow and measure the household sign rate (target 75% or better), autopay success and contractor willingness to pay 4%. Open a conversation with one CDFI or community credit union about a $250k participation for advances. Riskiest assumptions: whether households sign a contractor-issued agreement, and how to handle free-riders on a shared road, since the contractor can skip non-signers' driveways but not the common road. Also confirm lending and money-transmission licensing with counsel before Phase 2.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: PayHOA and HOA platforms: they sell to an association manager at about $2 per household, need an existing association, have no contractor side and no financing. Field-service and invoicing tools contractors use, such as Jobber-type products (from prior knowledge, unverified): they assume one billed customer, not 12 households splitting a road, and do not guarantee or advance payment. Group-payment apps like Venmo or Splitwise: no contract, no contractor payout, no recorded obligation. HOA lenders (banks serving incorporated associations, unverified): they require incorporated associations with financials, so tiny road groups are shut out, and we manufacture the collateral. DIY templates and attorneys: the legal formation is deferred until it unlocks cheaper credit, and delivered attorney-supervised. Maine statute and public districts: same, they are the legal substrate for the covenant, not a competing product. NC Private Road and Bridge Program: we bridge the cost share it demands. Local managers: potential partners for the lien-stage administration.

mutants.title: Daubert-Ready Sample Audits for Litigation Surveys
mutants.one_liner: A neutral data-quality auditor that gives survey experts and litigators a signed, control-calibrated audit of the respondent sample behind a Lanham Act, false-advertising or damages survey, or a teardown of the other side's sample.
mutants.customer: Wedge: the 30-60 US testifying survey experts and boutique survey-litigation consultancies who field likelihood-of-confusion, secondary-meaning, deception and conjoint-damages surveys, plus the IP and false-advertising litigation partners who retain them. Later: in-house counsel at CPG and pharma companies that run claim-substantiation surveys for FTC or NAD challenges.
mutants.problem: A litigation survey is only worth what survives cross-examination and a Rule 702 challenge. Until recently 'we removed speeders and failed attention checks' was an adequate answer on sample quality. Agents now pass those checks (99.8% of 6,000 trials in the parent's evidence), so the standard defence is hollow. Opposing experts can attack the panel, and the amended Rule 702 (Dec 2023) makes the proponent show reliability by a preponderance. Survey experts have no neutral way to show their sample is clean, and rebuttal experts have no fast, credible way to quantify contamination in the other side's produced respondent data. The fee is small next to the $50k-$300k+ a litigation survey costs (from background knowledge, to be verified in calls) and the case value behind it.
mutants.solution: Two case-driven products. (1) Proponent audit: before full fielding, insert canary and honeypot items (with the expert's sign-off) and run a pilot. Ingest detection signals licensed from dtect, Verisoul or DQC rather than building an ensemble. Field the test and control cells on a 150-300-complete slice of a licensed address-recruited panel (NORC, Ipsos or Verasight-style, resold, not built). Deliver contamination-adjusted net-effect estimates with bounds, a sensitivity table ('conclusion holds up to X% contamination') and a hash-timestamped chain-of-custody field log. A named academic methodologist signs a declaration that can be attached to the expert report. (2) Rebuttal teardown: a fixed-scope 10-business-day analysis of the opposing side's produced respondent-level data, built to fit rebuttal-report deadlines. The firm never opines on the merits (confusion, deception, damages). It only certifies or attacks data quality, so it is a supplier to every expert rather than a competitor.
mutants.why_now: Agents that pass attention checks (2025-26) killed the old defence. Pew's Aug 2026 finding of 18% bogus respondents in opt-in samples, with trap questions and Sentry disagreeing on who is bogus, gives opposing counsel a citable, public source. The Dec 2023 Rule 702 amendment gives judges an explicit mandate to scrutinise reliability. The first contested Daubert motion where an expert cannot rebut agent contamination will spread fast through the small survey-expert community.
mutants.revenue_model: $12-40k per case engagement (proponent audit or rebuttal teardown), billed to the law firm as consulting-expert cost and passed through to the client. $60-120k/yr retainers for survey-expert firms that run 8-15 surveys a year, covering unlimited pilots and field-log stamps. $2-5k per survey for a hash-stamped field log as a low-touch add-on. Later, a $25-50k/yr library subscription for in-house claim-substantiation teams. Gross margin is mostly the licensed control slice (about $3-8k per engagement) plus methodologist hours.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not paying for truth. The buyer is paying, with the client's litigation budget, for insurance against cross-examination, so willingness to pay is set by case value and not by the $/complete price that caps every other idea in this space. The test-versus-control design used in litigation surveys also means random-answering bots hit both cells and pull net confusion toward zero. Contamination therefore tends to hurt plaintiffs and help defendants, so both sides have a reason to buy: proponents to insulate, opponents to attack. Once a court admits or credits the method, it becomes citable precedent. That is process power and switching cost that no detection API can copy.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every survey expert named in published Lanham Act opinions of the last five years and 40 IP litigation partners. Run 10 price-validation calls (5 experts, 5 partners) and stop if fewer than 4 say $15k+ is reasonable. Days 10-25: buy about 300 completes each from 4 panel vendors on a classic Eveready-format and Teflon-format design, plus a 150-complete control slice from a licensed address-recruited panel. Measure how many bots it takes to swing net confusion by 5 points. Days 20-30: publish 'How many agents does it take to flip a confusion survey?' as a white paper and CLE talk proposal. Offer two free rebuttal teardowns on public-record survey data in exchange for permission to cite. Sign one academic survey methodologist as chief methodologist and testifier.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Detection vendors (Verisoul, dtect, Roundtable, CloudResearch, ReDem, CleanID) sell entry-time filtering to panels at cents per complete and produce nothing a court can use. They are input suppliers here. Data Quality Co-op's scorecard and Data Trust Score describe suppliers in general and do not give a case-specific, testifiable declaration.
